subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT AS TO NEW SYSTEM FOR SUPPLYING CIGARETTES TO PERSONNEL OVERSEAS
ANNOUNCEMENT AS TO NEW SYSTEM FOR SUPPLYING CIGARETTES TO PERSONNEL OVERSEAS
speechtext:
I wish to advise members of the house that, as a result of the combined efforts of the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of National Defence for Air, and myself, a new system has been developed for the sending of cigarettes from Canada to members of the armed forces in Italy which will result in the equivalent of air mail service.
It is hoped soon to have a similar system in operation for the members of our forces serving in Britain and France. The new system of handling cigarettes addressed to members of the forces in Italy goes into effect on June 19, and simply described, involves the sending by air mail of addressed labels, representing cigarettes ordered as at present in Canada to a Mediterranean depot, where they

Canadian Forces
will be drawn against a large reserve of cigarettes which has been built up over a period of time by bulk shipments.
Under the new arrangement, the individual sending the cigarettes is relieved of the possibility of loss between the tobacco company in Canada and the cigarette depot in Italy, as the Post Office Department is assuming responsibility for loss, if any, of the bulk shipments. In addition, it is expected that the new plan will result in a marked speeding up of deliveries. From the standpoint of the mailing public, there is no change in procedure. Orders will be placed in the same manner as at present, either with the tobacconist or direct with the company. When the company receives the order, a label covering each standard package of three hundred cigarettes ordered will be prepared, complete with postage and particulars. The labels will then be recorded by the Post Office Department and sent overseas by air transport. Upon arrival at the tobacco depot, the labels will be attached by members of the postal corps to parcels of the particular brand of cigarettes ordered and will then be dispatched to the addressee. The scheme has a particular advantage in that if any plane carrying labels is lost the labels can be quickly duplicated and the orders filled as if no loss had occurred. Replacement stocks at the depot in Italy will be forwarded in bulk shipment.
I have referred to standard packages of three hundred cigarettes. The efficient operation of the plan makes it necessary to adopt this size of a parcel, and after June 19 all cigarettes forwarded for men overseas must be in this size. The plan will not affect the present practice of certain auxiliaries, associations or other agencies sending bulk shipments of cigarettes for impersonal distribution to units or generally throughout the forces.
Orders for delivery under the new plan will be accepted for Sweet Caporal and Winchesters of the Imperial Tobacco Company, British Consols and Exports of W. C. Macdonald Incorporated; and Buckinghams and Wings of Tuckett Limited.
Persons wishing to order cigarettes from tobacco 'companies other than those mentioned may continue to do so, but in these cases the individual parcels will continue to be handled as at present. These orders also, however, must conform to the three hundred cigarette standard package.
As a further result of the scheme, it is anticipated that later on, possibly within a month, a system will go into effect whereby
members of the armed forces overseas will be able to purchase cigarettes direct from the overseas tobacco depots at the rate of three hundred for the equivalent of one dollar.

SOUTHERN ALBERTA DROUGHT AREA POLICY
speechtext:
1.	Will the government get a report from the P.F.R.A. officers regarding the conditions of the grain and grass crops and the stock watering places in southern Alberta?
2.	What steps are being taken to make use of the available water in the streams from the hills and mountains in working out some long term drought area policy in the above area?
Questions

subtopic: SOUTHERN ALBERTA DROUGHT AREA POLICY
speechtext:
1.	Through the field staffs under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and other departmental officers, the Department of Agriculture is kept informed of the crop and moisture conditions in Alberta. At the present time the district engineers under P.F.R.A. are making a check to determine the extent of the water reserves in the dams and dugouts in the Lethbridge and Medicine Hat areas.
2.	It has been recognized for a great many years that the best way to make use of the water supply of the streams of Alberta is by a series of storage reservoirs on, and adjacent to, streams where high flows and flood flows occur periodically, in order that such water can be held over and used beneficially when the stream flows are low.
The dominion reclamation service, recognizing the necessity of storing the high flows, made preliminary surveys of a great many storage sites in the foothills and mountains. The prairie farm rehabilitation organization have access to all of the information and plans made by the reclamation service and it has been the policy, as funds and staff have become available, to make detailed surveys of those various sites.
Until tests have been made to determine foundation conditions it is not possible to determine the feasibility of reservoir sites. This is the information now required in connection with all of those sites which have been already investigated by the reclamation service and the P.F.R.A. The policy of the P.F.R.A. is to continue investigations of storage sites on the mountain streams particularly with regard to foundation conditions.
In addition to these major works, planned for future construction, the sum of $366,384.66 has already been expended in Alberta under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act on projects designed to conserve and use the water of rivers and streams in Alberta.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION

speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, June 9, consideration in committee of Bill No. 135, to provide regulations enabling Canadian war service electors to exercise their franchise, and Canadian prisoners of war to vote by proxy, at any general election held during the present war, also to provide amendments to the Dominion Elections Act, 1938, which are consequential to such regulations, or have become necessary by the advent of the said war-Mr. McLarty-Mr. Bradette in the chair.
On schedule A, section 35-War service elector voting as civilian.

speakeroldname: Hon. N. A. McLARTY (Secretary of State):
subtopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it will be recalled that all other sections of both schedules were passed on Friday night. This was allowed to stand at the request of the leader of the opposition. The hon. member expressed apprehension that there might be a considerable number of men on furlough or on leave, and that if wider facilities could be given to enable them to vote, even though they might be some distance away from their ordinary voting places, it should be done.
I know it was the intention of the special committee which considered these regulations not to put any stumbling block in the way of those on leave or on furlough, exercising their franchise, and it was the committee's intention that they should vote in the most convenient manner. Over the week-end consideration has been given to the suggestion made. It must be remembered that the special committee broadened this regulation as widely as it thought possible, and there has been no suggestion of any attempt to curtail the right to vote of any war service elector. However, the chief electoral officer has given the matter consideration, and it is our belief that, without unduly complicating the machinery, through a slight amendment we can broaden it. Whereas under present circumstances a man in the army, the navy or the air force who is on furlough must report to the polling division of the particular branch of the armed services in which he serves, the schedule can be broadened so as to make it permissible for such member of the forces to vote before the election officer of any of the services, irrespective of the particular branch in which he serves. This change can be effected by striking out the words "of the same force" where they appear in line 44 of section 35 in the schedule, and inserting after the word "electors" in line 45 the words "by the commanding officer of a Canadian naval, military or air unit." I am advised by the chief electoral officer that this is about as broad as the provision can be made, if it is to remain practicable and workable. I believe in this we have gone some distance to meet the wishes of the leader of the opposition. To go further would make the provision impracticable.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext:
I move:
That section 35 of schedule A be amended by deleting the words "of the same force" in line 44 thereof, and by inserting after the word "electors" in line 45 the following words, "by the Commanding Officer of a Canadian Naval, Military or Air Unit."

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext:
Hon. members will realize that this amendment is the result of discussion which took place in committee on Friday night. It appeared to some of us that men who were on furlough for any extended length of time, during an election campaign, might be discriminated against because of their being at distant points, and their not being able to reach the places designated by the act as being the proper places at which to vote. I believe finally the matter came down to a consideration of those under twenty-one years of age who, by reason of the war services voting regulations, would have the right to vote.
Dominion Elections Act

Those over twenty-one years were, of course, covered by the general civilian provisions permitting their being sworn in in rural areas. I believe it may be said properly that the only possibility of inconvenience would be in rural polling divisions, because at urban points the possibilities of service voters obtaining their right to exercise their franchise conveniently would be greater. Therefore the discussion dwindled down to a consideration of those under twenty-one years of age in rural areas. The difficulty is one of covering only a small group so as to avoid discrimination against those in rural areas.
Although I realize that there is still a possibility of some discrimination and inconvenience, at the same time I believe the suggested amendment will meet the situation, and should reduce to a minimum any possible inconvenience to service voters on furlough. No matter where a man may be, there is apt to be a camp of one of the armed services nearby where a polling booth would be within his reach. Previously that might not have been the case, and great hardship would have been worked upon some who desired to exercise their franchise and who were under the civilian age limit for voting. So far as I am concerned the amendment is satisfactory, although in some instances inconvenience may be suffered. speechtext: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply) moved the second reading of bill No. 137, respecting surplus crown assets.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very important measure and one which I think de,serves a substantial amount of consideration before it receives
second reading. I regret I was unable to be here late last week when the minister introduced the measure. I am not as familiar with the subject matter as possibly I ought to be, but I am aware of the immensity of the problem that confronts the government and the nation in respect to the disposition of surplus crown assets. Some six months ago or so announcement was made of the establishment, by order in council, I assume, of a body termed the Crown Assets Allocation committee, and of the setting up by letters patent of a corporation charged with the responsibility of the disposition of these surplus assets. If that structure was already established by order in council with respect to the committee, and by letters patent with respect to the crown corporation, under I believe identical nomenclature, why was it necessary to come to parliament for legislation to do the same thing?-unless it be that the powers conferred by order in council in the case of the committee and by letters patent in the case of the corporation were not in the opinion of the government wide enough to take care of the situation.
Has the minister taken the house and the country fully into his confidence as to the immensity of the task, measured in terms of dollars and cents, which is before the corporation in the disposition of these goods? Has he told us why it has become so large as to be measured in terms of what I believe to be hundreds of millions of dollars-

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Billions.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Then I
suggest to him and the country that there has been default on the part of the crown in over-purchasing, in over-building and in oversupplying.
My understanding of the purpose of the Department of Munitions and Supply was that it was to be the one channel through which all requisitions for supplies from any of the spending departments were to be filled. I think that that principle is a sound one. It would never do to have government departments competing with each other for the purchase of similar classes of goods, or different classes of goods for that matter. Therefore I approved the principle of having one department set up to be responsible for the purchase of all supplies required for the great national effort of the country. There would be, I thought, coordination under that system, and there was a prospect, I hoped, of getting value for the money expended. But the weakness of the system as it developed was that the Department of Munitions and Supply has never had anything to say, or at

Surplus Crown Assets

least never assumed any jurisdiction, as to whether or not a given quantity of' this, that and the other thing was actually required. I believe that is borne out by the position which now confronts the minister, when he finds that he has on hand, not hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of goods, as I suggested, but, as I heard interjected, billions of dollars of surplus assets.
It must be remembered that all these goods have been purchased with funds obtained from two sources, either from heavy taxation imposed on the people of Canada, or from the heavy loans, amounting to six and a half billion dollars, which the Canadian people have contributed to finance the war effort of the nation. If it is now revealed that there are surplus assets which are not required to the tune of billions of dollars, then someone is in default.

The only complaint I ever made in that regard, and the minister I am spre will bear me out, was as to the allocation of some of the plants. We in the eastern part of Canada and in other parts have been denied them. But that is water over the dam. That is not the immediate subject of investigation. Apparently this thing got out of hand to the extent of hundreds of millions of dollars. The minister ought to give a full and frank explanation of the why and wherefore of that. I have heard that there were astonishing surpluses of some things. One day I happened to mention here in the house to the Minister of National Defence that I had heard of a surplus of 300,000 greatcoats. He questioned that severely, but he never gave me the figures of what the surplus was.

speechtext: A supply, but that is quite different from a surplus.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
-of 300,000 greatcoats-and how many more? I have heard that there was on hand a surplus-I am going to call it that-of literally thousands of dozens of tooth brushes, which we should know something about. Before this bill gets its second reading, and certainly if the minister cannot do it then he should do it when the bill comes into committee, the house and the country is entitled to have from the minister a detailed accounting to enable the public to determine whether value has been obtained for the money expended in days gone by.
We have had this question up before the house on more than one occasion, and the minister told us with a good deal of pride of what had been accomplished in the way of production. I think he is entitled to some degree of pride in the production of this country, and I am going to give him that credit. But he has never told us about the headaches which they have suffered in that department of his and: of the losses that have been sustained-I shall not say by any improper intent, because I do not mean that at all, but by lack of foresight, by lack of coordinating ability to determine what actually should have been done in a given case. There must have been many of these cases. I referred on a previous occasion to one of them. I am not going to refer to others that have come to my attention. But I do think that the minister ought to give us some information with respect to the huge volumes of money that have been spent in connection with these war expenditures and should indicate whether the country has got value for them or not.
Having read this bill, I have come to the conclusion that there must have been something in the order in council setting up the allocations committee, and in the letters patent creating the corporation, which was set up months ago and is now to be superseded by the corporation established by this bill-I come to the conclusion, I say, that there must have been something lacking, or something which in the opinion of the minister and his advisers ought to be in this bill. I find on reading the bill that this corporation and this committee is merely an instrument of the minister himself, that he is a dictator under this bill. There is nothing that this committee can do, or refrain from doing, there is nothing that this corporation can do or refrain

Surplus Crown Assets
3719>
from doing, unless it has the imprimatur of the minister. That constitutes him the sovereign controller aver the allocations committee and the corporation. Why was there any necessity at all for a committee?
Certainly we are not given much information with respect to this bill in the explanatory note which will be found opposite page 1. The bill starts out by saying that the several clauses contained in it are self-explanatory. I deny that statement. Of course, that is very general. The bill proposes, according to this note, to confer authority upon the corporation to be established thereunder, to sell, exchange or otherwise dispose of, hold, manage, recondition or otherwise deal with surplus crown assets and-this is the kernel, the reason for the bill-to confer certain powers upon the Minister of Munitions and Supply and the governor in council in relation thereto, including the power to establish an advisory committee.
Why the necessity of this crown corporation and advisory committee? The corporation is to be headed by Mr. Carswell, of whom everybody speaks well. I have not heard any criticism at all. The general manager of the company is a man who is well known, a man of managerial ability, who is being lent to or drafted into the organization, and who has had experience in merchandising and so forth. There is no criticism at all. A board of directors has been submitted, I believe, and approved by the ministry, the names of some of whom are well known to me and to most Canadians, and some of whom are perhaps not so very well known. I offer no criticism of the personnel of the corporation. If left alone I think they will do pretty good work. But what I am afraid of is that with the pressure, the political pressure-I might as well say at once what is in my mind

which is bound to be exerted on the minister just in the forefront of an election, this corporation will not be free from the pressure of the minister. Why is it necessary to have an allocations committee at all, unless it be for the mere purposes of assembling the information from the different departments? I can understand that that would be a profitable service and perhaps one which ought to be rendered.
I have grave fears about the working out of this committee, and I wish to devote a few minutes' attention to that. It is all related to the problem of the transition period between war-time industrial production and peace-time needs.
Certain broad principles ought to be laid down here by those in authority and be the
100-234i
subject of discussion, and be not only a guide to this corporation as to what they shall do with these surplus assets, but, may I suggest, and very properly so, a guide to private industry and as a method of control over this government agency.
The first thing I suggest to the minister is this, that through the agency of the committee, or by whatever other agency may be established, there should be an early inventory of accumulated stocks of materials. We ought to know exactly where we stand. The country should know-and there should not be anything secret about it-what are the accumulated surplus stocks of material on hand and what they cost.
There should be laid down as a second principle in relation to war-time production the reduction of production where all danger of shortage is past. We in this house do not know what the situation is, but I suggest to the minister, with respect, that he ought to provide parliament with a statement as to whether there is now any longer any danger of shortage.
The third principle I suggest is the cancellation or reduction of war contracts where it is evident that supply is ahead of anticipated demand and-this is for the benefit of the' Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell)-the diversion of man-power to industries where there is still pressing demand.
I see the minister has announced over the radio and in the press that there is to be a searching inquiry into the man-power situation, which has now reached an acute stage, and I can well understand that. But-this is by way of digression-he omitted in his statement to take into consideration the thousands of draft-dodgers in this country.

speechtext:
I should address the Chair. I apologize to the Chair, but the minister provoked that. I will return to the thesis I was trying to advance in a *constructive way.
This question of man-power is important. There should be, and I believe there will be, if Mr. Carswell and his general manager are left alone, a definite policy for handling surplus materials. I am glad to hear the announcement that a convention has been arranged between the two adjoining countries so that there will not be any dumping, one with the other. That is important and I congratulate the minister upon having made that arrangement. But what I am endeavouring to draw his attention to is this. The greatest care should be taken in the disposal of certain of those surplus assets-I refer particularly to tools, machines and the like- so that small plants shall not be crowded out of the picture for the benefit of the large plants. From time to time the Canadian people have allowed a great centralization of industry to grow up, and I believe it is not to the benefit of the body politic that that should have occurred. It has occurred to a much greater degree in the United States than here.
I remember travelling many times through the New England states. I have seen, and I am sure the Minister of Munitions and Supply has seen, because he comes from New England, the situation there. The three northeastern states, Maine, New Hampshire and Vermont, have been practically at a standstill because of the withdrawal from the confines of those states of small industries into the great industrial development of New 'England. They have been the hinterland of New England in the development of concentrated industry in the states of Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut and else-
{Mr. Mitchell.]
where. That has not contributed to the development of those three states, and the same thing is true in Canada. I realize, of course, as every thinking man or woman in this country must realize, why it has been so in Canada. Geography has to a large extent been the cause of the centralization of industry in Canada, and it may go on, but an honest attempt at decentralization ought to be made.
One of the things the minister can do- and I offer this to him with the best of good will as a constructive suggestion-is that in the disposition of machinery, in the distribution of equipment in government-owned factories, care should be taken to see that the small economic unit which will be on the market for new tooling and new machines is given an opportunity to buy some of this material. This must be done if they are to survive. Nearly every small industrial unit in this country will have to retool after the war because their machines are worn out after a long period of use without replacement. Then there is the question of obsolescence and the like. I do beseech the minister and his company to see to it that the small plants are not crowded out by the big baron with the ready money who will be able to outbid the other fellow.
Of course it is axiomatic-and I need only mention this general principle to the minister because I believe he is as fully seized of it as I can possibly be, and perhaps more so, since he has had a wider degree of business experience than I have had-that the disposition of surpluses should be made in such a manner and over such a period as to cause the minimum of disturbance to the normal market. If there is anything like a tendency to throw stocks on the market beyond the power of the market to absorb them, there is bound to be great disturbance to the normal business of the country. ,
The next principle that I suggest to the minister-and it has to do with something that is very near to government policy-is that stocks of materials should be utilized in such a manner as to reduce the danger of inflation. They should not be sold too readily. This principle ought to envisage a wide and equitable system of distribution of materials which have been definitely short for consumer goods because of war priorities. Above all, any attempt to comer the market by huge purchases of goods released from war uses should be prevented. Just imagine what might happen if one of the huge departmental stores in this country could go out and make a bid for one entire class or type of goods

Surplus Crown Assets
that the government have on hand. They would have the market for that class of goods. It should be prevented at all costs.
I am putting my next statement in the form of an interrogatory to the minister. What have the government and the Department of Munitions and Supply done to keep a check on these goods? Has there been integrated throughout in the rapid development of the department and the multiplicity of requisitions that have come from the three war service departments any system of inventory control so that they would know what was on hand at any given time? Has there been any compulsory reporting of supplies on hand from time to time? Is there any danger-I mention this without the idea of making any assertion with regard to it, because I do not know-of the existence of suppressed or hidden surpluses that nobody knows anything about? This has become so huge that it is quite possible there may be large hidden surpluses that the public does not know about. The allocation committee or the corporation itself should make a widespread and intelligent survey of the demand for materials for consumer goods, and wherever possible, owing to the shortage of consumer goods in Canada-I hear it spoken of everywhere I go-there should be an immediate diversion of surplus war stocks to civilian uses. We should not wait until the war is ended, when an unfavourable condition might be created. Of course if the war goes on for any appreciable length of time it is always possible, I suggest, to cancel all such diversions to consumer goods which may be required and return production to war needs.
Above everything else I warn the minister and his set-up-I am using the word "set-up" in no improper or derogatory sense-against sales to promoters or speculators. The minister will find the thrifty, the wide-awake man who will care more about making money than winning the war, ready to purchase these goods, and having in mind the scavengers in this country who are always looking for this sort of thing, he will find the man who will be out to buy these stocks on a speculative basis or promotion schemes. Sales should be made only to those who require such materials as are available or those who are creating plants to use them.
I wish to make another suggestion to the government. All this surplus war material was paid for out of the war appropriation funds. It has mostly, if not all, been added to the debt of the country. The net proceeds of all sales should be used to reduce the national debt. It should not go into current revenue. Any other method of allocating the funds to be derived from this source would be shocking
to me. To say that we will take the money that is derived from the borrowings made from the public and put them into the consolidated revenue fund, or make any other disposition of them save and except the reduction of debt, would not be prudent, would not be sound fiscal policy.
If I have time I should like to say a word or two about these war plants. Some have been closed down and reopened. To me that was significant, because it indicated at all events that the war was not quite over as some people seemed to imagine. I am glad that those plants were available for reopening and that they will supply the necessary munitions, let us say, to turn the scale in the last stages of the war.
A day is coming when these war plants will not be required for production purposes in the interests of the government. Of course many of those war plants are ephemeral in their nature; some, I hope, are substantial. Some I should think could be converted to-peace-time pursuits. I do suggest to the minister that all these plants are not mere scrap,, and any who get that idea into their heads should be disillusioned. These plants cost a great deal of money. They ought to be of great value, particularly their equipment, and they should not be sold at ridiculously low prices. They should be disposed of so that they may perform a useful purpose. I suggest, too, that careful consideration be given by the minister, in making sales of war plants, to the question whether they are adapted to conversion into peace-time industrial plants. There should be some planning in that connection on the part of the administration.
I do not desire to pursue this line of thought any further; I have given the minister some of the ideas that are running through my mind. I hope they may be of a constructive character, and that he will give consideration to them. At the risk, perhaps, of being misunderstood by some hon. members of this house I do suggest that there must be large quantities of surplus goods which would be of inestimable value to some of the occupied countries of Europe in the days that are to come. These goods have been paid for, and these people are destitute. There are those who lack food, clothing and other things. Canada has done much with respect to helping Britain. Canada now is doing something for parts of destitute Europe, and I think consideration might be given to the diversion of some of our surplus supplies from what might be glutted markets to lands overseas where there is to-day a crying need. In that connection the greatest care should be taken to see that these goods are not exploited by any
Surplus Crown Assets

international speculators. Let us take canned goods as an illustration. No doubt large reserve stocks have been built up for the armed services. Canned goods are in very short supply for ordinary consumers; I was at home over the week-end and that fact was brought forcibly to my attention. I suggest that strict control ought to. be maintained over these reserve stocks of canned goods so that they may be fed out to the consuming public and not to those who would make a profit by large purchases at small prices. They ought not to -be thrown on the market in large quantities, which would bring about the ruin of that portion of the agricultural population of this country which produces these commodities. There are very many pressing civilian needs to-day. Some of them can be met by wise *operation on the part of this corporation, to which, as far as I am concerned1, I would be prepared to give very substantial authority.
There is one point, however, I should like the minister to justify in connection with these *two bodies he is setting up. Why are they subjected to such strict ministerial control? If these men are worthy; if they are good business men; if they are given some guiding principles, then they ought to have freedom from ministerial control and authority which might very quickly degenerate, and I think hon. members will know what I mean. I dislike to see such dictatorial powers as are given in this bill conferred upon any minister in tonnection with a peace-time activity. It is a, delegation of authority we are making here to-day. The minister keeps all this authority in his own hands, and I think he ought to justify that position before this house. Then I believe he ought to tell us in some degree of detail the quantum of surplus goods they have on hand, their nature, variety and kind, and why such a tremendously substantial reserve, in terms of dollars and cents, has been built up. We ought to be assured that the money of the Canadian public has been wisely spent and not wasted, and that there will not be substantial loss. My fear is that because of over-purchases and because of what I believe to be a lack of jurisdiction on the part of the Department of Munitions and Supply to restrict quantities in the requisitions which it receives, there may be the possibility of some loss. It was like the old wartime information board when Mr. Lash was here. Information was fed in to him from a dozen or more departments, but he had no jurisdiction to edit any of it. That was a most unsatisfactory position for a trained publicist like Mr. Lash; he had no jurisdiction. Whether or not this department had the jurisdiction, and I do not think it had, it did not exercise

any by cutting down requisitions for what might appear to be inordinately large quantities of supplies. The minister should explain the position to the house before we accept this bill.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext: In listening to the opening remarks of the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) I could not help but think what fun it must be to be a cabinet minister. A few months ago, when the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) set up the War Assets Allocation Committee and War Assets Corporation Limited by order in council, he was roundly condemned by the opposition for proceeding in that way. The opposition said it should have been done by legislation and rightly so. Now, when the minister decides to supersede that action by order in council by bringing in a bill, doing this very thing by legislation, he is again condemned by the opposition.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is our privilege, is it not?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It is not only our privilege; I think it is a good thing the minister has yielded to the criticism of the opposition on this point and has brought in this legislation. so that it can be discussed in the house. But on that point I offer him my congratulations.
With regard to the argument the previous speaker sought to make in criticizing the bill because it placed too much authority in the hands of the minister, I want to say that this is a feature I welcome in the bill. I may be critical of the Minister of Munitions and Supply on many occasions; I may be critical of the government of the day, but I am much more anxious to see the democratically elected government which represents the people of this country control our economic affairs than to have control of those affairs improperly delegated to private business men outside this house and outside the government. So I say that on that point, too, I congratulate the minister; because it seems to me that what, he has written into the bill is not some dictatorial powers for himself, but simply the principle of responsible government with respect to our economic affairs.
Having said this, Mr. Speaker, let me turn to the other side of the picture and express some of the criticisms I should like to offer. I confess that those criticisms are directed not so much against the bill as against the policies that I fear may be carried out by the government under its terms. The other evening I was sitting in my office studying this bill, and

Surplus Crown Assets
had decided that of itself it was pretty much to the good. For a little diversion I turned on the small radio set I have in my room and, lo and behold, there came over it a familiar voice. It required only a moment to recognize the voice of my good friend the Minister of Munitions and Supply speaking from Port Arthur. I had been studying his bill, and thinking of all the good things the minister had done for the war effort following the principle of public ownership; then I had to listen to his voice telling me over the radio that after the war is over that principle must be discarded-

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: And in that he is absolutely sound.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
and full control given back to private enterprise. An hon. member to my right says, "Hear, hear." But I am sorry the Minister of Munitions and Supply is not prepared in peace time to stick to the principle he has found so necessary to meet the demands of war.
There are two or three points in the bill I would question. Perhaps it would be more appropriate if I were to wait until we reach the committee stage, later in the day, to make those observations. In general there can be no question as to the necessity for setting up some machinery to handle surplus war assets, which inevitably have been accumulated. I do not share the alarm of the previous speaker as to the quantity of supplies on hand. After all, these supplies had to be produced and made available if we were to carry on an all-out war effort. I imagine it is also true that a large portion of the huge figure to which the minister referred the other night would constitute plant and equipment financed by the government. When one realizes that there are huge surpluses valued at perhaps three or four billions of dollars, as stated by the minister last Thursday night, it is obvious that some machinery must be set up to handle them. That in itself is just occasion for parliament's passing such a bill as the one now before the house. The question in my mind however, is as to what policy the government is going to pursue under this measure when it becomes law. Is it to be the first concern of the government to protect the kind of economic system we had before the war, one which gave us the sad story of the thirties ; or is the government going to realize that the demands of peace are just as compelling as have been the needs of war? In the house, and throughout the country, that is the basic post-war issue.
I view under two headings the disposal of surplus assets. First of all there is a
quantity of movable goods, such as automobiles, clothing and other supplies. Secondl}' there is the matter of war plants, and crown properties such as the Polymer Corporation Limited and Research Enterprises Limited. In the same category there are certain aircraft factories, and there are many places where the government has part ownership of plants. That applies in respect of some aircraft establishments, and I believe applies also to the plant in Montreal which is to produce penicillin.
It seems to me that the disposal of the movable goods which will be surplus at the end of the war should be dovetailed into a national plan for the maximum production of peacetime goods. I feel that plants such as those to which I have referred, and some others, should be retained and operated by the government as part of a comprehensive national plan for the provision of full and useful employment and a maximum standard of living for our people. In other words, if I may repeat what I said a moment ago, we in this group feel that once the war is over, the needs of our hard-won peace must be faced with the same determination with which the country has faced the demands of war.
I know there are many in the house who insist that private enterprise can do that. When the Minister of Munitions and Supply spoke over the radio the other night he seemed to be suggesting that to the people in his constituency. But I hold in my hand a copy of a publication called Headlines; it is by no means a leftist publication. It is published weekly by the national association of real estate boards with offices at Chicago and Washington, D.C. This issue of May 15, 1944, contains an article dealing with post-war employment. The whole of it would be interesting, but I shall take time to read only one paragraph:
Who will find them jobs, especially returning soldiers? Private enterprise cannot by itself underwrite an employment programme which can be counted upon. No group of business men can assume responsibility for the entire national economy. We may want the government out of business, but whether we like it or not, mass unemployment is something that the government has to take care of.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: And the government cannot do it unless they can sell their goods.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
In contrast with the
statement I have just read, I have noted some interesting quotations in connection with the setting up of War Assets Corporation Limited. In its issue of January 29, Saturday Night made this comment:
The business community must be gratified that Mr. Horve (Minister of Munitions and Supply) has placed the disposal of surplus war asseto
Surplus Crown Assets

in the hands of business men and set them up in trade, not in political and official Ottawa, but in metropolitan Montreal.
The Financial Post of the, same date, January 29, quotes an address given just prior to that date by Mr. Carswell, the president of the corporation. This is what he said, in part:
Since the key job of the corporation is to protect the going economy against impingement of war surpluses, it stands to reason the corporation should never get into competition with industry-which is another way of saying it should not sell direct to the consumer but rather -to those whose legitimate business it is to deal with the article concerned and on a basis that, within the corporation's powers, will ensure reasonable profit to dealer and reasonable price to consumer.
I suggest to the Minister of Munitions and Supply that despite what his political or social or economic philosophy may have been when he was called upon to undertake the tremendous tasks of his present position, he took the view that the demands of war had to be met no matter how many readjustments were necessary in the economic set-up in order to fulfd that end. I contend that when peace comes the same attitude is necessary. When we are faced with the need of full and useful employment and the need of maintaining a high standard of living among our people, the primary purpose of a corporation such as the one being set up under this bill should not be simply to protect the going economy against impingement of war surpluses; its key job should be to meet the needs of our people.
There is one other thing that worries me a little, and I shall be quite happy if the minister can set aside my fears. I hold in my hand sessional paper 360 of May 28, 1943, dealing with optional purchase clauses in government agreements with private corporations. I shall read one or two paragraphs from this sessional paper which indicate terms of disposal. The following refers to one of the plants of Defence Industries Limited:
Defence Industries Limited is to make an offer if it desires to purchase the plant or any part thereof. If an agreement is not reached in sixty days, the government shall have a reasonable period to dispose of the plant to any other party on condition that it must be removed within ninety days from sale. If it is not sold to other party, the government shall remove the plant and level the site, or surrender ownership to the company without payment. The land is to be resold to the company for $1.
There is nothing significant in the last sentence, because I understand that in the first instance the land was bought for one dollar. But the rest of the terms seem to me to suggest that government policy with regard to the possible continued operation of a plant such as that is hamstrung by the authority

given to Defence Industries Limited under the terms of the contract. Here is another one with the Electric Reduction Company of Canada Limited:
The government shall offer the plant to the company at a fair and reasonable price. If not sold to the company within ninety days the company may dismantle the plant and deliver to the government at the plant gate.
That is an interesting way to put it.
Notwithstanding the foregoing, the company may purchase electrolytic perchlorate cell at a price equivalent to the market value of used platinum therein.
There are several other similar paragraphs in this sessional paper, but I shall not take the time to read them. When the minister speaks either on the second reading or in committee I hope he wTill refer to the question I have raised in connection with these terms of disposal. My desire is that plants in which public money has been invested for the purpose of meeting the needs of war may continue to be operated by the government to meet the needs of our people in times of peace. My fear is that these terms block the carrying out of such a policy-if perchance we can persuade the government so long as it is in power to carry out such a policy.
This question cannot be handled on a piecemeal or patchwork basis. The house and the government should realize, as probably the government has, that the whole question of disposing of three or four billion dollars' worth of assets is not something isolated that can be handled without regard for the whole economic set-up of the country. When one contemplates the magnitude of these surpluses that are to be disposed of, and thinks of them in terms of trying to fit them into the whole economy of the country, he is brought right up against the necessity of our getting a vision of really rebuilding our economy and remaking Canada once this war is over. It ranges out into the whole question of a tremendous housing programme, the rebuilding of our cities, the seeing to it that there is work for those who come back from -overseas and for those whose services in the making of munitions will no longer be necessary. To hope that private enterprise will be able to do that is, I suggest, sheer folly. I have given at least one instance in which a private enterprise journal realized that that is the case. The government looked at the needs of war and realized that they had to be met, and my contention is that the people of Canada will expect that same approach and that same attitude when peace comes.
This is indeed a most important measure.
I look upon the bill itself as being in the

Surplus Crown Assets
nature of enabling legislation. It does not indicate just what the government's policy is going to be. Perhaps that is correct in the nature of things. As I said earlier, I welcome the fact that the final say in these matters will be in the hands of the government of the day, that that is not being delegated to private business interests. However, because of the importance of the policy that will be carried out under this bill when it has been passed, I hope that during the discussion the minister will give us some indication of the policy the government will follow. I still hope he will say something a little more encouraging than the remarks I heard from him over the radio [DOT]the other night.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the minister is to be [DOT]congratulated upon introducing this bill at the present time. I believe the majority of the Canadian people will agree that there is a need for such a bill. Certainly it would be inadvisable in the highest degree to allow the situation to run wild, so to speak, when peace is declared. We must take every precaution to see to it that there is a return to as nearly normal as we shall probably be able to get after so colossal a conflict as the one in which we are engaged.
Reading through the bill I find it on the whole quite satisfactory. The principle is sound, as I have said. Before mdking the few comments upon it that I think it fitting I should make, I probably should revert to the remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Knowles), for whom I have a very high degree of respect. As I gathered the general purport of his contribution, it was that since the government had found it so necessary to take over control of industry in large measure during the war, and because of that measure had been able to attain so high a degree of success, it argued automatically that government ownership in peace would solve our problems. I think that some extremely important factors are being overlooked when any such conclusion is drawn.
May I point out to my hon. friend and to those who are disposed to think as he does that in war our primary problem is production. In peace our primary problem in an age of plenty is distribution. Government ownership will enable the government to produce with the greatest success. But government ownership will not enable the government in time of peace to distribute; for distribution depends upon the amount of purchasing power which goes into the hands of the people and the degree to which that purchasing power is spread out among the people so that they can consume the goods which are being produced
by industry. That mere fact should give all people who are socialistically inclined in their thinking cause for a good deal of serious reflection. In war time not only is the government obliged to get quantity of production but it must have design, and many times the particular design which the government-wants is not a profitable type of production for any industry to be engaged in fabricating. The government must have design, and it must have special quality; it must also have an exceedingly high degree of speed in the production of the items that are being brought into existence, and at the same time there has to be a high degree of secrecy. All these things make it so that government ownership is probably the best producer in this field in time of war.
But in peace time these factors are not nearly so important. There is no need for secrecy. There is no particular need of a high degree of speed unless people are buying goods faster than the goods are being produced, and that is not likely in an age of plenty. There is no particular worry about quality, because if people have the money they will simply leave unpurchased the goods that are unsatisfactory in quality. Quality therefore will take care of itself. If there is a sufficient demand for goods, industry will provide the speed, because the faster they produce the goods the more money they will make. So that those who argue for government ownership in time of peace are falling into error; for all these factors will be taken care of by industry itself. The solution of the problem of distribution is to provide purchasing power for the people. If we can manage to give high enough wages, good jobs, good enough prices for the things which are produced and reasonable prices for the things which people have to buy, pensions and allowances and all that kind of thing which will allow the rank and file of the people to buy abundantly of the goods which industry stands ready to produce, then we shall be successful in distribution, and the ownership of the industries will simply make no difference at all, provided that industry manufactures the goods, which it will, and sells them, which it certainly will.
Having dealt with that matter in some measure, may I turn to certain aspects of the situation which I think it is well to point out to the minister. I remember that when I first came into parliament I received in the mail one day a fine shoe which had been cut all down one side with a razor so that it was impossible to repair it and make it fit for use. The shoe came to me from somewhere in Nova Scotia, and the man who sent

Surplus Crown Assets

it to me wrote an exceedingly indignant note in which he said, "There are literally thousands upon thousands of shoes which have been treated like this and thrown on heaps, while thousands of people in this area need even shoes such as this and are denied the privilege of obtaining them." That kind of wanton waste I am sure the minister wants to put himself in a position to prevent. We certainly do not want anything like waste or sabotage after this war. The people need the goods, either people in our own country or people abroad, and provision' must be made for allowing the common people who have been deprived of these good things to get them after the war. Never mind if that will be competing with private industry. Some provision must be made to protect private industry if that is necessary. But the goods simply must not be destroyed.
There is another aspect of this whole matter to which the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) referred the other night and which I should like to mention briefly. I think it is in a high degree desirable that provincial governments should have the privilege of buying these war assets in so far as they may desire to do so. I can conceive that great numbers of tractors, trucks and the like might be of much value to the provinces in their public works programmes. They ought to be made available to the provinces at a very reasonable rate, and the country ought to know that that is going to be done. The provinces should be able to buy enough of these assets for a future supply if need be. I use tractors and trucks merely as an illustration.
Again, municipal governments ought to be able to obtain their needs of such equipment and machinery in so far as they may desire to do so. They should certainly have a chance to bid along with the governments of the provinces.
I think that after the last war there was far too much secrecy with respect to the disposal of surplus war material. I speak subject to revision of my opinion after learning more about the situation, but at the moment I fail to see why at the close of the war the government should not publicize in the widest and freest and frankest fashion the exact amount of goods which they have for disposal, telling the people where these goods can be obtained, how they can be obtained, at what prices they can be obtained, so that everybody may know all about them. It seems to me that that would avoid the possibility of the scavengers, to whom the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) referred, having a field day. With the radio facilities at the disposal of the

government and with newspaper advertising it ought to be an easy matter to conduct a campaign of publicity so that everybody will know all about a thing which is everybody's business.
May I turn for a moment to the degree of control which has been placed in the hands of the minister. I am not a friend of centralized control. I think we have far too much of it. I was sympathetic with the words of the hon. member for York-Sunbury when he advocated decentralization of control. I think that the time has come when the whole country must study means of the decentralization of industry, the decentralization of credit control and of responsibility with respect to everything that pertains to our public wellbeing. So I say that I am not in favour of having too much power centralized in the hands of the minister. Yet in this case I believe it is a good thing. I notice at least four clauses in the bill which give the minister great power. I think, with certain reservations, that that is sound under the circumstances. It is sound because it centralizes executive capacity and is likely to work for greater efficiency in the disposal of this material, which will be a titanic job, I think. Then, it will centre responsibility on one man so that we can get at him and parliament will be able to get control of the situation much better, inasmuch as the minister will have that responsibility. At the same time, I think the minister will agree that there should be provision for establishing checks against his power. I am not saying that this will be necessary in the case of the present minister, but no one knows who the next minister will be and I am sure that the minister as a citizen of Canada would feel much better if this tremendous power were safeguarded with adequate reservations which would reassure the people that such power would be exercised wisely and in the public interest.
I suggest that some such set-up as this might be introduced into the bill. I would not go so far as to suggest that the minister modify the present bill, although, if he saw fit, he might do that; but some such measure as this I do suggest-that each provincial government should be given a considerable amount of influence in controlling the whole policy. The minister would do what members of the government in large measure have done during the war; he would invite into his confidence the representatives of the provinces for advice and counsel and put a certain amount of work on them in carrying out the purposes of the act. If that were done the minister would be in a better position to carry on. If he were to ask each province to appoint a com-

Surplus Crown Assets
mittee to work with the war assets corporation and with him, and if then each provincial government were to ask the main municipalities in the province to appoint committees to work with it, we would have once more an opportunity for the widest measure of publicity and understanding regarding the matter.
I believe that in the days following the war there will be great necessity for maintaining confidence amongst the people. They must not be permitted to get the idea that they are being "sold down the river," or that things which are not in their best interest are being done behind the curtains. I believe that the making of such an arrangement as I have suggested, under which the provinces would work with the central government and the municipalities would work with the provincial government, would serve as a. sort of safeguard against undesirable public attitudes regarding the whole matter of the disposal of war assets.
I have said all that I care to say at the present time. Such other observations as I have I will make when the bill is in committee.

Has the minister had any reports from the hundred and one companies-I am using an arbitrary number- which have been set up in connection with the making of munitions, in regard to stocks and various lines of materials that have not been used and which there is no likelihood of using?

speechtext:
The committee itself is closely in touch with every department of government. Munitions and Supply have a representative on the committee, and it is the duty of that representative to know the situation in every plant in Canada, regardless of whether it is a crown plant or a private concern using government materials, and to watch for surplus inventories. That is done now, and was being done before the corporation was formed. Material was being transferred from one plant to another. The department goes further than most private firms in keeping inventories of all materials. On the termination of contracts the department moves quickly to arrange that surplus raw materials from the contract are removed from the plant and disposed of to other plants. Now surpluses will be reported to the committee, and disposed of through
War Assets Corporation. I receive eight or ten recommendations from the committee each day. I understood the hon. member to ask whether there were any reports under section 3.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Am I right in assuming that there are large quantities of material the purchase of which was ordered and which are in store in various manufacturing companies-goods that would have been used for making munitions had changes not been made in certain munitions equipment, which changes rendered obsolete large stocks of material?

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: There are occasions when changes of specification make obsolete certain materials, either semi-manufactured or raw material. It has been the practice throughout the munitions programme to dispose of these surplus materials as rapidly as possible. If they are capable of use for any other purpose they are used for that purpose. If they are not, they are converted to scrap and sold back to the primary producers. That has been going on constantly. Within the last six weeks arrangements have been made to the end that the War Assets Corporation will handle all disposal of scrap, and all rendering back into scrap. Before that, the director of scrap metal, in the organization of the Department of Munitions and Supply, did that work. All surplus material or material rendered obsolete was reported to the director of scrap material, and it was his duty to have it rendered back into scrap and sold to primary producers.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I have in mind some first-class material which has been rendered obsolete in certain plants owing to change in the design of munitions they are making, but which could be used in various other plants or to fill civilian requirements. Is someone specifically charged with the duty of salvaging obsolete material instead of scrapping it?

speechtext: Yes. The director general of production has taken that duty on himself. He has general knowledge of the programme of the department, and he decides whether material of the type the hon. member mentions can be successfully used by another plant. If so, the production schedule is arranged in the other plant to use that material. That work has been going on under careful direction.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Or disposed of for civilian requirements.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It can be, yes. We have not been selling material outside the department, except scrap. We have been transferring' material from one programme to another, but we have refrained from selling to the public.
Surplus Crown Assets

The purpose of- this bill is to authorize the selling of any surplus material to the public. It is a very serious responsibility to sell government property to the public. Public property is always regarded as in a class by itself, and any wrongful disposal of it is regarded as much more serious than ordinary mishandling of materials; therefore, great care has been taken to safeguard the sale of such material.
At the present time all surpluses of the type that were previously handled by transferring from one contract to another will be reported first to the committee, and by the committee ;to the minister, and then transferred to the Crown Assets Corporation for expert disposal which the machinery of that corporation can apply.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: What type of inspection is carried on to determine what shall be scrapped and what shall not be scrapped? I had a very disturbing report from a responsible individual ^employed in a government-owned plant oper-:ated by a private company. I would not care to mention either the individual or the company at the moment but I can do so to the minister. This individual reported that in a great many instances machine parts which could have been readily repaired were relegated to the scrap heap and sold as scrap. subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The acceptance of war material is in the hands of the United Kingdom and Canada inspection board. The rejections by the board become, of course, the property of the contractor. subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I was not speaking of parts delivered from the factory where they are manufactured, but rather of parts that had become damaged as a consequence of use and discarded when they could be repaired. speechtext: My hon. friend is talking of a machine tool?

speechtext: That problem has engaged the attention of the department. We have a company called Cutting Tools and Gauges. I can assure the hon. gentleman that the point in question is not being overlooked. Mr. FRASER (Peterborough West);: What I had in mind was that some garage men may want machine tools after the war is over. I wondered if they would have any knowledge that the machines they require may be for sale?

speechtext: Machine tools are listed. They are in a class by themselves. The disposition of them is an important problem, because the government's purchases amounted to about $100,000,000. The same scale of depreciation is applied as is allowed by our income tax department on machine tools used in a factory. The price is definite, depending on the history of the tool. These tools are listed as they become surplus and the lists are widely circulated. Small plants are given preference. One condition of sale is that if the plant is being sold to replace an old tool then the old tool must be rendered into scrap and disposed of. The purpose of selling machine tools is to improve the equipment of small plants first of all and not to put a lot of obsolete and inferior tools on the market in consequence.

speechtext: Some of those tools have been imported from the United States and other countries?

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The minister did not speak on the second reading of the bill, but I hope he will take an opportunity to reply to some of the points raised in the speeches that, have been delivered. I remember that the hon. member for York-Sunbury referred to the short life of War Assets Corporation Limited, and he wondered what the main reasons were, why that method was changed to this one based on legislation. Perhaps it might be appropriate under this section for
the minister to give us some description of what has been accomplished in the seven months during which War Assets Corporation Limited has been in existence, what it has handled, what it has disposed of, the methods it has used and whether those methods will be continued under this corporation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
In the order in council setting up War Assets Corporation Limited it was stated that a bill would be presented at the next session of parliament providing legislation to replace the order in council. The purpose of the legislation is, first, that the principle involved may be discussed in this parliament. As I said before, the sale of government property is a serious matter, and I believe hon. members should be made well aware of the procedure. I think it was stated in Bernard Baruch's report that the disposal of government property should be conducted in a gold-fish bowl; that it should be open to, public view, and that will be the procedure of War Assets Corporation Limited. Another reason, this is a continuing job. The powers of the government under the War Measures Act will expire shortly after the war ends, but the work of disposal will continue for a long: period thereafter. An act of parliament i& desirable to provide continuity.
It was suggested by the hon. member for York-Sunbury that great surpluses are now available for disposal. Of course that is not the case. It was thought desirable to provide the machinery for disposal while the problem was on a small scale, and to build up an-organization to cope with the larger problem whenever it might confront the government. I mentioned the amount of $3,000,000,000. I arrived at that figure having regard to the-fact that my department has purchased about $10,000,000,000 of munitions and supplies, and I estimated that perhaps one-third of this would be subject to disposal at the end of hostilities. Many of these munitions may be outside Canada, in the United Kingdom, on the continent or in other allied countries. Mutual Aid material is subject to recall after the war, if it has any value. We have ships around the world, being operated by various people, and these will be subject to recall. We have warships, not all of which will be required for our peace-time navy, and that will become a problem of disposal. We have guns and other weapons used by the armed forces, and a wide variety of other supplies. To give hon. members an idea of one problem, this country has produced over six hundred thousand automotive vehicles. Many of these will not return, but a considerable proportion will be brought back, and that will be one great problem which will have to be-
Surplus Crown Assets

faced by the War Assets Corporation. That corporation is charged with keeping in mind that it is disposing of the property of all the people of Canada, and its first duty is to see that the material is distributed in such a way that all the people will share in any benefit that may accrue to our economy through the sale of this used government material.

Directly to consumers,
does the minister know?

Then the scrap and salvage division, which .has been under the direction of the corporation for the past month, sold $88,000 worth of scrap, while another agency of the department, which is also being transferred to the [DOT]corporation, disposed of $132,000 worth of scrap. subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: At reasonable prices?

speechtext: No, I have not that information. subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
How many motorcycles have been disposed of already? While I am on my feet I should like to ask the minister what method of identification is used in connection with government-owned property. I have in mind such machines as lathes. I am not blaming the minister for

this; I am just drawing it to his attention. I recall having visited some aircraft and shipbuilding factories, and I was told that the only government identification was a number painted on the machine. To remove that number would require only a little gasoline or something of the kind. For their own protection I should think the government would have some metal stamp on each machine, so that in days to come, after this disposal is completed, no one may be accused of possessing property to which he has no right. If the government had a permanent identification mark a check could be made, which would eliminate the possibility of anyone getting possession of government property to which he was not entitled. I refer to motorcycles, because not long ago I was told by certain people, who I thought were in a position to know, that quite a number of motorcycles in good condition had been sold for very small sums. I remember that in one case $250 was mentioned. I was surprised, because I did not know that there had been permission given to sell the motorcycles. I was in doubt as to whether the government had gone so far as to sell them. Apparently, however, this Indian motorcycle with sidecar was sold for $250, a reasonable price for anyone to have to pay.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. member has spoken about the identification of machine tools. He will be aware that it is difficult to steal a motor car and then to camouflage it in such a way that the ownership cannot be ascertained. Machine tools are just as well protected. I think the hon. member could assure anyone who has a government machine tool that it would be only a matter of time when the owner thereof would catch up with him. Careful registration is kept of every machine tool. There are several identification marks, including the name of the manufacturer, on each tool. The government will not hesitate to prosecute for theft anyone who illegally possesses any unit of crown property. We have had one or two cases of theft, and in those instances have prosecuted and recovered. That will be our policy, and it is one which I believe is generally known. I would be surprised if there is any wholesale illegal transfer of crown assets. Then, so far as motorcycles are concerned, I believe the only motorcycles handled by the committee have been transferred from the army, through mutual aid, to Russia. I know of no sale to the general public. I must point out, however, that there was in existence an army disposal board, before the corporation was formed, and it is possible that that board sold motorcycles to the public: If so, I have no knowledge of it.

Surplus Crown Assets

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
When I questioned the minister the other night I understood him to say that property, as defined, includes crown plants, as well as other kinds of equipment. In the event-and the minister knows I hope this will not happen-of the decision being made to dispose of a crown plant, what course would be followed? I understand that most of these crown plants are held in the name of the Minister of Munitions and Supply. Does that mean that he would report to the committee and that committee would report back to him, or what procedure would be followed?
In that same connection, would the minister give some indication as to what would happen in connection with plants where expansions have been made, with government financial assistance, and where the plant managers tell us there is no clear line of demarcation between privately-owned and government-owned property.
Then, will the settlement of terms of disposal, such as I read a while ago from a sessional paper, No. 360, come under the jurisdiction of the machinery we are now setting up?

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The machinery for the disposal of crown plants is that the department responsible for the plant declares it surplus to the requirements of that department. This is reported to the board, and the board examines the situation to see whether any other department of government can utilize the plant in question. If not, recommendation is made to the minister with respect to disposal. That is, if no use can be found for it for government purposes, a recommendation goes to the minister that it be turned over to War Assets Corporation, as surplus crown property. The minister, in turn, would receive the report and, after consideration, make a recommendation to council. It will be remembered that every decision involving values over $15,000 must be reported to the governor in council. If council decides that the plant in question should be disposed of, such plant would be turned over to War Assets Corporation for disposal.
My hon. friend suggests that every plant owned by the government should be operated by the government. The leader of the Social Credit party said, very properly, that in war time the problem is one of manufacturing, while in peace time it is one of disposal of output. He suggested that if there were plenty of money in the hands of consumers there would be no problem of that kind. I can assure him that the problem would still be there, because Canada is capable of producing
almost anything in quantities far in excess of the ability of her own population to consume. Our exports always represent a very considerable part of our annual production.
I believe there are certain plants which the government could operate to advantage; but there are a great many plants the government could not possibly operate in competition with private industry. When those plants become surplus to government requirements, the option will be either that the plants be closed or that they be put into hands which can operate them successfully. The decision is, as I say, first in the hands of the committee, and then in the hands of the minister. The matter is then considered by council and, if disposal is decided upon, the actual disposition will be handled by the corporation.
The hon. member has referred to certain types of construction where the method of disposal is specified in contracts. The situation is not as serious as he believes. It arises where a special war munition or a product required for war munitions can be built much more cheaply as part of an existing plant turning out a commercial product. The option usually is to spend a fairly small amount of money in building a publicly owned addition to a privately owned plant, or spending a large amount of money in duplicating the privately owned plant, and adding to it a unit required for war production.
The hon. member referred to one plant which I recognized as Defence Industries Limited. That was a case where the raw material in question was chlorine. A plant to manufacture chlorine is expensive to build. While I forget the product to which the hon. member refers-although I recognized it at the time-I remember it was a product used wholly for war explosives. The best way of obtaining it seemed to be that of building a unit inside the plant of D.I.L. The unit built by the government had no relation to the private business of D.I.L.; it was not a commercial product. Therefore D.I.L. had a perfect right to say, "This may be all very well for the war, but the material you are making will not be used after the war, and we want that unit removed from our works. It does not fit in with an integrated chlorine plant." A proviso was made to the effect that D.I.L. would make us an offer for the unit, with such conversion as might be possible. If we were not satisfied with the offer we could then sell the unit where we liked, and under that condition remove it from the property. That type of transaction has been made only when it was the cheapest way to provide the particular war material. I am satisfied, and
Surplus Crown Assets

I think the committee will agree, that the procedure taken was the cheapest way for the government to achieve the required result.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
