speechtext: In the case the minister has just described I take it that the War Assets Corporation would not have anything to do with arriving at the price; that would be determined already by the terms of the contract?

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was sorry to be out of the chamber when the hon. member for .York-Sunbury was speaking, but with most of the arguments I heard and with the suggestions offered by others who followed him I readily agree. I am not going to discuss the question of war plants because I shall leave that to those who know more about it than I, but I should like to say a word with regard to. training centres and other places where there is not much in the way of equipment but where there are many buildings.
Farmers all over this country have been in dire need of lumber for several years. Their buildings have gone into disrepair and are becoming worse every month. They have accepted all this in good spirit because of the war. I suggest that in the disposal of buildings at the training centres the farmers should have preference in every possible case. I do not think any jobbery or speculation should be permitted in the disposal of these buildings; if possible, they should be sold direct to the consumer; that is, to the farmer. Just how this is to be done is perhaps outside my knowledge, but I wonder if a selling agent could not be posted at each of these centres to have control of the sale of the building. He could deal direct with the individual where possible, or perhaps auctions could be held. But in any event, the sale should be direct to the consumer and the farmer should not be asked to pay tribute to any other firm or dealer. I urge this suggestion upon the department.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The hon. member has described the exact method contemplated for disposing of that type of equipment by Surplus Crown Assets Corporation. Very few buildings have been turned over to the corporation, but the machinery is such that sales will be made on the ground to users in the vicinity, who can get greatest value from the salvage.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: This new corporation will not be confined to war assets; I take it that it will handle all surplus property?

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Of the government.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: And also that it will be continuing in its nature. That is to say, it will not have to do only with surpluses that arise after the armistice is signed; it will continue to operate indefinitely as long as there is any use for it. I take it that the minister or his department will be the chief provider of information, although there will be some obtained from the various defence departments.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Each member represents a department w'hich is likely to have material for disposal. In the long run the Department of Munitions and Supply will perhaps be the smallest source of material. At the moment we are perhaps the principal source. The termination of contracts is a function of the department, but any scrap or salvage arising out of the termination of contracts will be for disposal by Surplus Crown Assets Corporation. The departments of national defence will ultimately be the largest sources of material to be handled by the corporation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: What about goods still in process of manufacture under contracts with munitions and supply? Is this section broad enough to cover material in process?

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE

I presume it would be automatic, but we may find ourselves in the position where a minister receives a report which he does not care to pass on to Surplus Crown Assets Corporation. Why should that not be provided against?

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is the minister to be allowed no discretion?

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am just wondering whether all surplus assets should not be made known to Surplus Crown Assets Corporation. As one hon. member has said, we may have a different minister.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Surplus Crown Assets Corporation is represented on the committee by the president. The committee may recommend that assets be declared surplus, but the government may know of reasons why it does not wish to declare those assets surplus. It may be a matter of government policy.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Unless the minister felt it wise to pass the information on, the committee

Surplus Crown Assets
might not know. There is nothing in this section which makes it mandatory upon the minister to pass on that information which is given to him by the various departments. I should think the minister would have no objection to giving the information filed with him to Surplus Crown Assets Corporation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: As long as the minister is satisfied. I do not see anything in the bill which would relieve the minds of those in business which might compete with products declared to be surplus. Business should know whether these surplus assets are to be held off the market or whether they are to overhang the market for some indefinite time until the government or Surplus Crown Assets Corporation decides to dispose of them. For instance, there might be thousands of yards of duck and business might not know just when the ultimate disposal would be made. That material would be overhanging the market and would have a depressing effect on trade.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The only protection the businessman can have is the calibre of the management of Surplus Crown Assets Corporation. The business of the corporation is not solely to protect trade; it is to recover government money, and to distribute the goods turned over to it to the best interest of all the people. It must combine all three interests in a reasonable way. It has power to hold or reconvert and operate as well as to sell. The matter of disposal requires the broadest judgment of almost any problem. My hon. friend will know that after the last war, material was sold by auction, and much of it got into the hands of speculators and second-hand dealers, with a tremendously destructive effect on industry and without any real benefit to the crown or to the public. We believe that the machinery now established will bring to bear on the problem the best judgment that can be found. The purpose will be to bring about a balance between the various interests that must be considered.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
What is the fundamental philosophy behind this bill. A short while ago the minister said that in Canada we can produce far more than we require and that therefore we have to export a great deal. Now he is saying that the chief purpose behind this bill is to get as much out of the surplus assets as possible, whereas many of us will feel that the main thing after the war will be, not to try to salvage what we can out of the surplus material, but to create jobs. That will be in
the minister's mind also. So that in relation to the question which I asked before, I should like to know whether industry will find that there will be in some cases huge surpluses of material overhanging the market and awaiting a buyer at the best disposition which can be made of it by a government company, or whether industry will know definitely what the policy of the government is to be in regard to this material. Will prospective buyers know that they cannot get this material below a certain price? Will the government even hold some of these surpluses as strategic materials or something of that kind? It seems to me that we ought to know what is to be the prime essential, whether it is to create jobs or to salvage to the last dollar, because the two may conflict with each other. So that it is well to know what is behind this bill in that regard.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The purpose of the bill is to bring the best balanced judgment that can be had to bear on problems of that kind. My hon. friend would hardly expect me to say now that we would do one thing or another thing as a matter of general policy. Business will be able to discuss its problems with the management and directors of the corporation, just as will public interests. I think business generally believes that the machinery, now being established will serve the purpose as well as any that can be devised.

subtopic: PROVISION FOB CORPORATION AND .ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
If Surplus Crown Assets Corporation follows the policy which the minister outlined a few moments ago in reference to the disposal of crown plants, that policy will create a lot of jobs and I support the minister's policy in that regard exactly 100 per cent. I wholly disagree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I should like to tell him as one who was through a lot of this following the great war and has seen the results that followed the disposal of government plants and their purchase by private capital just what happened, for instance, in one case. We have to get back to private enterprise just as rapidly as possible, and I hope that this example of the results which followed from the disposal of one government plant after the last war will make some impression on my hon. friend. I have had a lot to do with business, and with big business, and I am afraid my hon. friend has not. The minister spoke of the disposal of plants. Immediately following the last war-I do not just remember what agency was set up for the disposal of crown plants, because it is quite a few years ago now-there was a very large plant on Dufferin street, Toronto, in which aeroplanes had been made. It was a substan-
Surplus Croton Assets

tial, well-built brick plant, well proportioned, well engineered and well machined in every particular. That plant was disposed of in some way, together with much of the goods and equipment therein. Some private company of investors, as I remember it-I am not just sure of the financial set-up-purchased that big plant, with the result that in a short time perhaps fifteen different new industries . started up in that plant. When I say fifteen, that is an arbitrary number; there might have been a few more or a few less. But about fifteen new industries started up in that plant, some of which are perhaps there to-day, and they gave much employment.
The minister is right in his policy of disposal of crown plants, enabling .private investors to buy them or in any event to use them and start up scores and scores of new industries. We want all the new business we can get, and there are many, many businesses which are not started simply because they lack the .plant in which to start. The plant I have in mind is one I know very well. It was next door to the plant with which I was associated. I saw the results of the disposal of that plant. My hon. friend the member for York South is thoroughly familiar with the plant I am speaking of and with the facts I am presenting to the committee. Ever since the last war a large number of men and women have been engaged in different lines of industry in that old plant. It is old now but it was not old at that time. That is what we want, to get back to private industry as quickly as we can and produce the requirements of the people. It cannot be done economically by government plants, as the minister very well said.
Besides, a large number of these plants have been built along lines which private industry would not follow. It did not make a fig of difference if it took one thousand tons or one hundred tons of coal a week to heat some of these huge government .plants, because they were put up for a temporary purpose, and no doubt the cost of heating in many of these plants is excessive. I * am not finding fault with the government for that, because the plants were put up for a special purpose, to help win the war. But the cost of heating is excessive in many cases because the buildings are not of brick. Private enterprise, when it puts up a plant, counts upon occupying it for an indefinitely long period of time and figures on the cost of maintenance, heating and so forth. We did that in the business with which I was associated. We put up a substantial plant, because private enterprise always looks to the cost of maintenance and heating, coal to-day being a very large part of the cost of production.

So that I say to my hon. friend the member for Winnipeg'North Centre that I do not want him to feel that I am basing my disagreement with him on anything but sound argument and many years of experience. My experience has been that many government plants would not be purchased by private industry. Shell constructed .plants, for instance, would not be purchased) by private industry because the buildings are not substantial enough. A substantial building might be purchased by private enterprise, just like that big aeroplane plant that I mentioned on Dufferin street, Toronto. That is the kind of thing we want. We want to give more employment, and I know of no place where we can get more jobs more quickly than by getting back to private enterprise as quickly as possible after the war and by the government disposing of substantial plants.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT

speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide:
1.	That sums not exceeding eight hundred million dollars ($800,000,000) -be granted to His Majesty for the purpose of making war supplies available to any of the united nations, other than Canada, and of fulfilling any obligations arising out of the united nations relief and rehabilitation agreement;
2.	That the governor in council may determine the terms and conditions upon which such war supplies are made available to any of the united nations and may require in certain cases payment or repayment in kind of property or reciprocal action or provision of supplies or other direct or indirect benefit as may be deemed appropriate;
3.	That the Canadian mutual aid' 'board be authorized to carry out the purposes of this resolution;
4.	That the governor in council be empowered to raise by way of loan under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, such sum or sums of money not exceeding in the whole the sum of eight hundred million dollars ($800,000,000) as may be required for the purpose of defraying the expenditures herein mentioned and for purchasing or otherwise acquiring or 'procuring war supplies in Canada through the agency of the Minister of Munitions and Supply, the principal and interest of any such loan to be a charge upon and payable out of the consolidated revenue fund.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the essential purpose of this resolution and the bill which will be based on it is simply to extend the scope of the Mutual Aid Act to include the provision of relief supplies to UNRRA and to appropriate $800 million to carry on our mutual aid programme. The borrowing powers which are added are normal provisions of all our war appropriation measures.
Parliament last year overwhelmingly approved the principles of our Mutual Aid programme. Parliament has already this year-with practical unanimity-approved Canada's participation in UNRRA and the principle of using Mutual Aid funds to make this possible. I believe parliament and the vast majority of Canadians approve these

Mutual Aid
principles now more than ever before. The events of the last few days have brought home to all of us the critical nature of the present phase of the war and the vital importance to all our forces of full supplies of the best fighting equipment. Our Mutual Aid programme has helped substantially to arm the British forces that fight side by side with our men in Normandy, in the channel, and in the skies of France. Mutual Aid has been helping to arm the Russian forces whose achievements have made victory possible and kept many Germans from being ready to destroy our forces landing in France. Mutual Aid is helping to rearm the French forces, so that they may fight effectively alongside our men and others-as in Italy-in the liberation of their countrymen whose spirit has stood fast against many terrors during the last four long years. Mutual Aid has been helping the Australians to drive the Japanese back from island to island in the Pacific. Mutual Aid supplies for our long-suffering friends in China have recently arrived in India and will go through to China by air or by land, as soon as that is possible. Mutual Aid supplies are flowing to all the major fronts. They are enabling Canadians working here at home to give the strongest possible support to our men in uniform by strengthening their comrades in arms and thereby contribute most effectively to the speeding of victory.
The essential purposes and principles of Mutual Aid remain as they were determined by this parliament last year, with only the addition that we propose to include in Mutual Aid the provision of essential relief supplies to our liberated allies. These will be contributed through UNRRA, the democratic, international organization that has been created for this purpose.
The general principle of mutual aid is now well established among the united nations. The United States pioneered in the field with the enactment of the lend-lease act even before she entered the war. The lend-lease principle has now become not only a great "weapon for victory," but a household word and a landmark in relations between nations. Britain has applied the lend-lease and mutual aid principle in providing military supplies to various allies requiring aid from her. Australia and New Zealand, while originally on the receiving end of lend-lease, are now providing reverse lend-lease to the United States on a scale which is very large in relation to their population and resources. The acts of our own parliament occupy an honourable place in the evolution of this new and sensible form of
inter-allied relationship. Our Mutual Aid programme is an important part of a larger whole.
The main purpose of Mutual Aid is to ensure that Canada's war production-made possible by the bounty of nature, the hard work of our people, and our good fortune in being far from battles and bombs-is used most effectively in the common cause, in accordance with the strategic needs of the war. It is intended to make this most effective use of our production possible without the creation of huge inter-allied debts, which would burden commerce after the war and prejudice a just and enduring peace.
The ways in which these purposes have been accomplished and the principles of Mutual Aid put into practice are made evident in the report of the Mutual Aid board, covering its operations up to March 31 last, which my colleague, the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), as chairman of the board, has tabled this afternoon. I shall not attempt to recapitulate the detailed information in the report, nor to summarize it, in moving this resolution. I wish to refer to some parts of it, however, in commenting on a few of the major questions that are relevant to our present discussions. The Minister of Munitions and Supply, as chairman of the board, is in charge of the administration of its work and will be able, if necessary, to provide further information to the house.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), on March 16 of this year, tabled in the house the general Mutual Aid agreements which Canada had entered into with Britain, the Soviet Union and Australia. Later the agreements with China and the French Committee of National Liberation were also tabled. These agreements, which are practically identical in form except for minor adaptations to fit special circumstances in the case of the Soviet Union, set forth the general terms and conditions upon which Mutual Aid supplies are furnished by Canada to her allies. The Prime Minister himself explained the nature and purport of these agreements when he first tabled them, and called attention to several important aspects of them. A copy of the agreement with Britain is appended to the report of the board, and the others are in practically the same terms. This agreement itself is short and quite easily understood. I believe, therefore, that I need not attempt to enter now upon any exposition or explanation of these agreements, or of the terms and conditions upon which Mutual Aid supplies are furnished.
By the time the Mutual Aid Act was finally passed in May of last year, the government had already begun to establish the administra-
Mutual Aid

tive organization necessary to put it into effect. The board began immediately to work out the new arrangements with other countries which would be necessary as a consequence of its operation. However, it took longer to put the Mutual Air plan into effect than we had expected, because of two essential features of the plan. The first was the principle that we would contribute actual supplies rather than money to the countries receiving aid. The second principle was that we would make arrangements directly rather than indirectly with countries receiving aid. In order to contribute actual supplies, it was necessary for the board to arrange to have these supplies produced and purchased on its direction and for its account, and then to transfer the supplies to the recipient nation. The principal changes required were in the operations of the Department of Munitions and Supply, which had formerly been acting as an agent of the British and other governments, and which now had to become in effect a, dealer in war supplies, having them produced at the direction of the board, which took title to them, paid for them on delivery, and then turned them over to the recipient country. To put those new principles into practice it was necessary for the Department of Munitions and Supply to take over the great bulk of all the thousands of war contracts placed by the British government with Canadian producers through the agency of the department in the past. This was a formidable task, involving much legal, administrative and accounting work. The take-over of these British contracts went into effect on September 1. The corresponding date for the take-over of Australian contracts was October 1.
To establish direct arrangements with Russia, China and the French Committee of National Liberation has also taken considerable time. Not only was it necessary to secure details of the supplies required-which it has been difficult for the French to furnish-but it has been necessary for the board and its various administrative officers and agencies to make inquiries and hold many consultations to verify the essentiality of the requirements, the possibilities of supply and of transport, and to avoid duplication with the programmes of Lend-Lease and Mutual Aid supplies being furnished by the United States and Britain. This administrative work and organization of the board, necessary to carry out the purposes and meet the conditions of the act, are described in the report and I need not go into it here. I would like to assure the house, however, that care is taken to ensure continuing consultation not only -with the military and supply authorities in Canada, but also with the various combined

boards and other international military and civilian agencies concerned with these questions in Washington and London.
War supplies have been furnished as Mutual Aid to Britain, Russia, China, Australia, India, and the French Committee of National Libertion. Detailed information on the actual supplies furnished to these countries up to March 31 is given in the report-particularly on pages 15, 22, 26 and 29. There is no simple way to summarize those many physical items. In the case of Britain they cover the great range of our production of munitions and military equipment, ships, and food and farm products. In the case of Australia they include air training services for Australian airmen, munitions and aircraft supplies, metals, timber, automotive equipment and other items, as well as the services of Canadian ships required to transport supplies to Australia. In the case of Russia, the major items have been metals, explosives, vehicles, repairs and services to merchant ships and in particular wheat flour, to which the Russians have given a high priority. For China the outstanding items are guns and ammunition-both small arms and light artillery-together with the signal equipment and motor transport necessary to complete the artillery batteries. We have also provided Canadian shipping services to deliver these supplies to the Chinese authorities in India. Supplies had only begun to be provided to the French committee by March 31, but at the present time there are substantial shipments ready in depots to be despatched to the French as soon as final shipping instructions are received from them.
The figures for shipments up to March 31 are not representative of the proportions in which supplies are now moving to the various countries. It took longer to arrange Mutual Aid supplies for Russia, China, the French and even Australia, than it did for Britain, and consequently their total share in shipments has been increasing in recent months. Countries other than Britain will, therefore, receive a larger share of the total Mutual Aid supplies this year than last year.
Mutual Aid expenditures have inevitably lagged somewhat behind the shipment of goods, as the board makes payment to the Department of Munitions and Supply only after delivery, and it takes some time for the invoices to come in and for the necessary verification of accounts. Of course, under war conditions the actual shipment of goods is not held up until the accounts are settled. As a consequence, the value of the war supplies furnished up to March 31 is in excess of the expenditures made-particularly in the case of

Mutual Aid
supplies for Russia, Australia and China-and there were, of course, outstanding accounts at March 31 remaining to be paid.
The expenditures up to March 31 out of the Mutual Aid appropriation are shown in the table on page 7 of the report. It will be noted that, when rounded off, the figures are approximately as follows:
Expenditures for war supplies transferred to Britain amounted to 724 million dollars, to Russia 23 million dollars, to Australia 21 million, to China 4 million. Relatively small sums of $874,000 were expended to send essential supplies of flour to the West Indies and $482,000 to send wheat to India, to help relieve the famine which developed there last autumn.
In addition, expenditures for war supplies held by the board in transit or storage and to be transferred in future to recipient countries were 139 million dollars.
Expenditures for administration were approximately 25 thousand dollars.
The total of all the expenditures was approximately 913 million dollars.
Out of the billion dollars provided by the original act, there remained therefore at March [DOT]31 approximately 87 million dollars. Most of this was expended during April in meeting commitments previously incurred. Ten million of it had been set aside for UNRRA, in accordance with the authorization of parliament in the UNRRA Act which the house passed on April 21.
Considerable detail is given in the report for the expenditures made for supplies for each of the recipient countries. As it is conveniently available to the house and the press, I will not burden the house with it now. In the case of Britain, it will be noted that expenditures of $555 million on munitions and military supplies are classified under 13 headings, while expenditures of $169 million on farm products and foods are classified under 19 headings. In the case of Britain, estimates are also given of the funds which Britain herself has spent in Canada during the year, which exceed quite substantially in total the Mutual Aid expenditures on supplies for Britain. These figures cannot be given in such detail as those for Mutual Aid expenditures, because we do not have the detailed information. I would also like to emphasize strongly that these figures for British expenditures in Canada and the similar figures for British receipts from Canada are only estimates, subject to a margin of error.
I would like to emphasize clearly that these Mutual Aid shipments are not by any means the only war supplies going to the United Nations from Canada. All the countries receiving Mutual Aid, with the possible exception of China, purchased supplies in Canada
during the past year. Those able to pay for substantial amounts of supplies have been making substantial purchases. Some nations have been able to pay for all their requirements in Canada, and as a consequence they have not requested assistance under the Mutual Aid Act. Our sister dominions, South Africa and New Zealand, though obtaining substantial quantities of war supplies from Canada, have not asked to secure any portion of them as Mutual Aid. It is possible that some countries, because of new developments-perhaps because they will need more from Canada or because their ability to purchase will be less- may make application for the first time this year.
The board has followed the policy of providing as Mutual Aid only what the recipient countries were unable to pay for in Canada. As far as a country is able to pay, it buys what it requires. In the case of Britain and, indeed, in the case of all the other nations in the sterling area, their purchases during the year ended March 31 have substantially exceeded the value of supplies provided to them under Mutual Aid.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Do we determine which country can pay and which cannot?
Mr. 1LSLEY: Yes, we know pretty well.
Figures are given, as I have already indicated, in the report to show how this has worked out in the case of Britain. The table on page 19 shows the estimated payments to Canada by the United Kingdom in the year in question under various headings. It will be noted that payments for munitions and military supplies amounted to 353 million dollars. A further quantity of munitions, as indicated in the footnote to the table, estimated to amount to about 90 million dollars in value, was purchased in effect by Britain through drawing upon the funds which she had previously paid into the munitions production revolving fund, which was used for financing the production of munitions in government-owned plants in Canada. I will not burden the house with the other items in this table, but I would call attention to the fact that Britain purchased from Canada during the year a larger value of foodstuffs than we provided to her under Mutual Aid. I would also point out that metals, lumber and certain other products for Britain were all purchased rather than included in Mutual Aid supplies, mainty because of administrative reasons. It was not considered desirable to extend the Canadian procurement machinery, particularly that of the Department of Munitions and Supply, unnecessarily into the purchase of goods which Britain had previously been obtaining directly from Canadian contractors.
Mutual Aid

The sources from which Britain derived the funds to make the purchases which I have described and other payments to Canada are shown in the table on page 19 of the report. It will be noted that roughly half of the ,funds Britain obtained during the year and used in Canada came from payments made in Britain and to the British government by the Canadian forces overseas. These payments, as the hon. members will note if they compare this table with the one given in Hansard last year, were more than double the corresponding payments made in the previous fiscal year. I would expect a further substantial increase in the current year now that our forces fire engaged in intensive operations. I should also call attention to two other sources of funds which enabled Britain to purchase supplies in Canada. It will be recalled that last year we undertook to buy out the interest of the British government in Canadian war plants. Part of the transaction took place before April 1, 1943, but 165 million dollars were paid to the British government in the early months of the last fiscal year. There is another and somewhat more complicated group of transactions described in the report as "Cash withdrawals from working capital funds formerly advanced to the Department of Munitions and Supply and contractors". When the Department of Munitions and Supply was acting as the agent of the British government in placing contracts in Canada, the working capital required for the production of supplies for Britain was furnished by the British government, and amounted to quite considerable sums. When, however, the various British contracts were taken over by the Department of Munitions and Supply and became Canadian contracts from which deliveries could be made either to Britain, or to Canadian forces, or to any others of the united nations, the Department of Munitions and Supply took title to all the goods in process and itself provided the working capital funds required to finance the production of the goods in question. The British government was therefore able to use the working capital which it had formerly advanced to make current purchases during the year.
The new element in this year's mutual aid bill, which will be based upon this resolution, is the extension of Mutual Aid to cover Canada's contribution to the united nations relief and rehabilitation administration-or UNRRA, as it is called. The house is already familiar with the nature, purposes and activities of UNRRA, which were discussed in April when the house passed the act approving Canada's participation in UNRRA and ratifying the international agreement by which the

organization was established. I do not propose, therefore, to attempt to explain to the house the way in which UNRRA is organized nor any details of its operations or proposed operations. The parliamentary assistant to the President of the Privy Council, who dealt with many of the questions in the earlier debate, will be able to answer further inquiries regarding UNRRA wrhich may come up in discussing this resolution or the bill.
Prom what has already been said in the house, I think we are all-or nearly all- agreed upon the essential importance of providing aid and relief to our allies, who have suffered so greatly under the occupation of the enemy and from the immediate effects of hostilities in their homelands. We recognize, too, that we in Canada have food and clothing and medical supplies which can be furnished to our liberated allies to help them over the very difficult period before they are once again able to provide for themselves.
It is appropriate to note here certain points concerning the size and nature of Canada's contribution to UNRRA. While some of the countries receiving relief will be able to pay for it in foreign exchange, many will not be able to do so-and what they are able to pay to UNRRA in their own currency will likely be needed in part for local expenses and in any event cannot be converted into dollars, or used to purchase supplies abroad. Consequently it was provided in the agreement establishing UNRRA, which the house has approved:
In so far as its appropriate constitutional bodies shall authorize, each member government will contribute to the support of the administration in order to accomplish the purposes of article 1, paragraph 2 (a) (i.e., the provision of relief). The amount and character of the contributions of each member government under this provision will :be determined from time to time by its appropriate constitutional bodies. All such contributions received by the administration shall be accounted for.
At the first meeting of the council of UNRRA last November, the method of determining the contributions of members was carefully considered and the council made the following recommendation, which was supported by the Canadian delegates who had consulted.the government on this matter:
As to the amount and character of the contribution of each member government, to be determined by its constitutional bodies as provided for in article V of the agreement, the council recommends that each member government whose home territory has not been occupied by the enemy shall make a contribution for participation in the work of the administration, approximately equivalent to one per cent of the national income of the country for the year ending June 30, 1943, as determined by the member government.

Mutual Aid
The council recognizes that there are cases in which the recommendation above may conflict with particular demands arising from the continuance of the W'ar or may be excessively burdensome because of peculiar situations, and therefore recognize that the amount and character of the contribution recommended is subject to such conditions.
In accordance with this recommendation, we are proposing to make a contribution to UNRRA equal to one per cent of our national income for the twelve months ended June 30, 1943. I have obtained from the dominion bureau of statistics an estimate of our national income-and I would emphasize that it can be only an estimate-for this period, which they have compiled in such a way as to be as comparable as possible with the estimate prepared for the United States by the United States department of commerce, on which the contribution of the United States is to be based. This estimate of our national income turns out to be approximately 7,615 million dollars. Based upon this estimate, we are proposing to make a contribution to UNRRA of 77 million dollars. Already parliament has authorized the government to provide an amount up to ten million dollars from the Mutual Aid appropriation of last year, and the appropriation now being asked under this resolution will enable us to make our total contribution in the figure I have indicated. I should point out to the house that the council of UNRRA has recommended that not less than ten per cent of the amount contributed by each member government shall be in such form of currency as can be expended in areas outsidle the contributing country, and that the * balance shall be in the form of a credit in local currency which will be available for the purchase of the contributing country's supplies and services. Therefore we shall be providing to UNRRA ten per cent of our contribution in a form which UNRRA can transfer into foreign exchange if it so desires.
In extending our Mutual Aid Act to include the provision of relief supplies to our liberated allies we shall be extending the purpose for which supplies are furnished under Mutual Aid to include not only the effective prosecution of the war but also the securing of a just and enduring peace. Already Mutual Aid, as I have shown, has contributed and is contributing to the winning of victory. We can look forward with hope and confidence to the role which Mutual Aid will play, through our contributions to UNRRA, in relieving the human suffering which the war has caused and in helping by constructive measures truly to secure a just and enduring peace.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Bradette in the chair.

speechtext:
This resolution is very
similar to those that we have passed in bygone years since the introduction of the Lend-Lease principle has come into our economy, and, of course, particularly in time of war we all desire to aid other countries by supplying them as far as we possibly can with necessary munitions of war and foodstuffs. On that account it seems to me that the measure is admirable. As we have passed the bills in days gone by, and coming now to this resolution, I cannot help thinking that there is involved here a principle which we so often hear opposed, namely, the idea of giving something for nothing. I wish I had thought of this Mutual Aid resolution when talking the matter over with the Minister of

Mutual Aid
Labour the other day when he referred to the principle and said that he had held all his life the belief that one should never give something for nothing. The fact of the matter is that in this $800 million provision what we are actually doing is giving a large part of it away to other countries. Of course, it has to be bought, but it is bought by ourselves through a certain process of lending. As I understand it, in the passing of this resolution, and of the bill which will follow, we are giving the government power to raise by way of loan under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act an amount in the neighbourhood of $800 million. It means that a very large portion of that will be an expansion of our own credit here and will be a bill chalked up against the Canadian people.
I am not going to oppose that either. As far as I am concerned, perhaps there should be more of it done, because we all recognize that after there is an expansion of credit in our internal economy it is reflected in the prosperity of the people, since the people share in that expansion of credit. It goes into their pockets in one way or another and they are better off. Where the rub comes is that if it is ever to be paid off the people of Canada will have to pay it. If it goes into the debt structure of the country and is handled by a process of refunding, the debt may remain for centuries, and even then the Caandian people will be called upon to foot the bill, so far as interest is concerned.
I hope we shall not hear so much, in connection with any proposals made from this group, about the principle of giving something for nothing, because this is. a measure which entertains that principle. It is giving something for nothing to other countries. We could reverse the order, if this country ever found it necessary to do so, and do the same thing, only instead of shipping goods out, we could make them available to our own people.
I am quite conscious of the fact that many of these goods may be regarded as surplus. If we have a very fine crop of wheat this year I do not know whether that commodity will be included, but there is no harm that I can see in giving away goods to these countries that need them. The only thing is that we pay for them here in one way or another. As a matter of fact, when we do something of this kind the country is richer financially though, of course, it is poorer as far as actual wealth goes, because whenever you export you send out real wealth. You may expand your credit and be financially better off, but when you do so there is a corresponding debt.
I would ask the minister a couple of questions. Just what is the meaning and what is the force that he attaches to the word "mutual"? I do not think I have that properly analysed in my own mind. Do I understand that it is a Mutual Aid bill in relation to other countries doing the same thing? If that is so,
I would couple another question with that one. I should like to compare anything we are doing with what perhaps the United States is doing, and to know how it works out on a per capita basis, if that is possible. We have twelve million people in Canada who are now offering to supply $800,000,000 worth of goods to other countries. How does that work out on a per capita basis, and what is the United States' share in this Mutual Aid idea? If twelve million people in Canada are responsible for the sending out of the country of $800,000,000 worth of goods and if it is really Mutual Aid, it would appear to me that the United States would have to send a lot more than that. The hon. member for Red Deer reminds me that it would amount to something in the neighbourhood of $8,000,000,000. I should like the minister to answer these questions. I am pleased to concur with others in allowing the first reading of the bill to go through, provided that we discuss it on second reading to-morrow. On page 8 of the report I find this statement:
In the agreements which the nations receiving Mutual Aid have concluded with Canada there is provision for Canada receiving such reciprocal aid as may be determined from time to time in the light of the development of the war.
What is the meaning of this at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
The agreements provide that Canada may obtain as reciprocal aid such articles, facilities, services or information as the nation receiving Mutual Aid is in a

Mutual Aid
position to supply and as may be determined by common agreement in the light of the development of the war. This provision will be of benefit to us should the war develop in such a way that at some time in the future we require a greater value of goods and services from any of the countries receiving Mutual Aid than they require from us. In such circumstances we would be able to request reciprocal Mutual Aid. Up to the present, however, we have not needed to obtain reciprocal aid in goods and services, because all the countries with which we have been concerned have needed a much larger value of supplies from us than we have needed from them. To have requested them to provide us, as reciprocal aid, with part of the supplies we purchase from them at the present time would only reduce their ability to buy from us and increase the size of the excess to be provided by Mutual Aid.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
The usual procedure is that the country desiring Mutual Aid makes application to the Department of External Affairs. The qualifications for Mutual Aid are checked by external affairs and by the treasury department and the country is approved as a recipient of Mutual Aid. After that, applications for specific items are filed with the administrative officer of the Mutual Aid board. Such items are cleared by him with the agencies in Washington and with our own chiefs of staff as to essentiality, and if approved in both quarters they are submitted to the Mutual Aid board in Canada for approval. After that, orders are placed through the Department of Munitions and Supply in the
Mutual Aid

case of munitions, or through the Department of Agriculture or the Department of Trade and Commerce in the case of foodstuffs. In most cases deliveries are made at a port in Canada. Goods for China, however, are delivered to their destination by Canada.

Looking at the problem as a whole; bearing in mind that Canada was sending flour to the United Kingdom and1 that the United Kingdom was sending back a certain amount of flour to the West Indies, it seemed reasonable that instead of Mutual-Aiding all the flour to Britain, we could Mutual Aid a certain amount of flour to the West Indies. I do not think we have done any more for Great Britain in this war than Great Britain has done for us. The hon. member may have a different view about it, but I do not think so. I explained fully to the hon. member for Macleod, I thought, the basis for the use of the word "mutual". It is based upon the fact that when a nation sends its

Mutual Aid
men out, and those men lose their lives, they are doing something for the common eause- just as we are, when we make machines, and so on, and contribute them to the war. If the hon. member suggests that it must be machine for machine, then it is the same as dollar for dollar, and the whole principle of Mutual Aid or Lend-Lease disappears from the picture entirely. Nations have been trying to get away from this idea of cash on the barrel-head, and material value for material value. They have reached the place where they think that if we are to win this-war we have each to do everything we can in our own countries.

Mutual Aid

I Mr. Howe.]

subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT

That is the reason why I
asked what my hon. friend meant by asking whether it is the same. speechtext:

Drills	 1,000

With regard to the question raised by the hon. member for Rosedale, that certain goods were offered some nations who were in a position to pay for them, I am wondering if there is really a demand for these articles. The reason why I bring this question up is the fact that in Britain with one-third of the cultivable land that we have in Canada they have as many tractors as we have, and at the commencement of the war one-third as many. That may be good business; I do not know. At any rate, reference is made here to a number of different pieces of machinery. With the great shortage that exists in this country-and, as I have pointed out many times before, many people in Canada had orders and permits passed for drills for this spring which they have not been able to receive at this date, some time after seeding is over-I am wondering how these requests are arranged. Are they done through the Department of Agriculture in the old land, and is there a check-up to ascertain whether these commodities are essential at this time when production is hampered in consequence of man-power shortage and the shortage of labour-saving machinery?

subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext: During the past two years it has been thought that, solely from the viewpoint of winning the war, it is more advantageous to have foods grown in the United Kingdom than in Canada. My hon. friend knows that when the submaiine war was at its height, shortage of shipping was very serious. For that reason, during the past two years we have shipped a considerable amount of agricultural machinery to the United Kingdom. We did so because we believed that this woujd prevent the British people from starving, and if it caused some inconvenience to our own people, that is not a very serious impact of the war on Canada.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT

speechtext:
I understand that the
Lease-Lend programme started with the $/00 million loan to Britain against which no securities were actually taken; following that there was a gift of one billion dollars to Britain, and following that, a gift of one billion dollars in Mutual Aid, without any arrangement that anything should be returned; and the present basis upon which this resolution will be passed, with the bill succeeding it, is the same. Is it not a fact that this was an arrangement agreed upon as part of the general war programme, where Canada did embark on a course peculiar to Canadian economy and Canada's war programme, and quite different from all the rest? The $700 million no doubt was similar to the Lease-Lend programme of the United States, because that $700 million was used to buy goods in Canada; but the remainder, totalling now roughly three billions in three years-two billion up to date and an extra billion now- is an out-and-out gift from Canada in Mutual Aid, without anything being expected in return. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext: If our requirements from Great Britain exceed her requirements from us she is obligated under these agreements to furnish Mutual Aid to us. What the hon. gentleman says is substantially true, namely, that from the material point of view we are contributing, as I would say, to the common cause-

subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext: And as best we can.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Yes. It goes to Great
Britain, a lot of this, but it is really a contribution to the common cause rather than a gift to the United Kingdom.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Well, of course, the significance of that contribution of Canada to the common cause is that with the $700 million lent to Britain and the two billions already given in Mutual Aid, that comes roughly to three billions. Contrasting that total contribution from Canada with the total from the United States, our Lease-Lend programme is much more substantial proportionately to our population than the Lease-Lend programme to the south of us. There may be some people who feel that Canada should not make that kind of contribution. I believe that the great majority of Canadians will be proud of the fact that Canada is making that contribution and will be glad
Mutual Aid

to continue it so long as we can make it to the common cause and the struggle in which we are engaged. The only thing about it is that there are not many people throughout Canada who appreciate, in addition to the war programme that Canada is carrying on, the enormous contribution that Canada is making in this programme to the common cause, in proportion to her population and her industrial wealth.
There is one more observation in regard to the common contribution which I desire to make, and that is the fact- that we are financing it ourselves. That is true, is it not? We are financing it without any aid either offered or expected in so far as the goods are produced and in so far as they are prepared for shipment to wherever they are going. The financial responsibility of providing the capital and the medium of exchange required is a purely Canadian enterprise. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
That is correct.
Mr. MeGEER: And in that, I believe, we have found an indication of Canadian financial independence of all the world. If we can do that in war time and use our own financial power to make an enormous contribution to the cause of world freedom, we must never forget, when peace comes, that we Canadians do not have to go hat-in-hana into the financial markets of the world to borrow foreign capital to build Canadian institutions.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Vice versa.
Mr. MeGEER: My hon. friend says, "vice versa." I realize that it would be extremely difficult to get any lessons of this kind across to that side of the house. Just what "vice versa" means, I do not know; but when I am talking about Canadian financial independence I am talking not about something that has .any vice versa about it.

subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
All vice.
Mr. MeGEER: This is one definite Canadian programme that has nothing to do with anything else. We have been taught for a great many years by that kind of nonsense that we did not have the means to finance ourselves. We had to borrow in Berlin; we had to borrow in London; we had to borrow, in Paris. We were a young country and we had no means that comes out of the accumulated wealth of the ages; but when this crisis came it was not the wealth of London that counted. We happened to be the rich uncle right here in Canada.
There is another observation I should like to make to the minister. If we could only speak as boastfully of what we are doing for old age TMr. McGeer.]
Canadians as of what we are doing for Mutual Aid in the cause of common freedom there would be a great many Canadians just as proud of that-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: APPROPRIATION OF $800,000,000 FOR WAR SUPPLIES TO UNITED NATIONS AND OBLIGATIONS UNDER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Order.
Mr. MeGEER : -as they are proud of the splendid contribution we are making. I do not want to traverse that subject any farther, but I did rise in my place to emphasize the fact that our Mutual Aid programme is something of which every Canadian has good reason to be proud.

speechtext:
That may be true; probably
it was not provided in the order in council which established the machinery. A separate order in council set up the committee; but that would be on the recommendation of the minister, which would include the names and designations of the members of that committee. Another government could change the composition of the committee if it wished to do so.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: As I see it, there is nothing in the bill that would prohibit the crown assets allocation committee and the board of the War Assets Corporation from being the same personnel.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: They could be, if the government wished.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Is there any special motive in using the languge of this section, which says that the minister, with the
-zsm
Surplus Crown Assets

approval of the governor in council, may do certain things? My understanding of the draftsmanship of bills of this kind is that usually power is given to the governor in council. In this case, however, it seems that the minister is the initiating authority and the governor in council comes in later by way of reference. Is there any special reason why that should be?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I think it only puts the actual procedure into words. The governor in council does not originate anything itself; everything is recommended by some member of council. It may be the Prime Minister, but usually it is the minister in direct charge of a particular effort. In this case the minister recommends and the governor in council approves. In the bill the minister is given certain powers which he may exercise of his own volition, while certain other powers must have the approval of the governor in council.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I take it that the personnel of the present crown assets allocation committee will be continued when this legislation takes over and the order in council ceases to operate?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: As I understand it, the principal duties of the crown assets allocation committee is to advise the minister after having ascertained what there is to sell. Does that committee advise at all as to how it shall be sold, or where?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Then what is the function of the board? What does the board do?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The board does the selling.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It merely does the
selling?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The committee can recommend to the minister a scale of priorities. For instance, if it is dealing with road machinery, it can recommend that first priority be given to a province, second priority to a city and third priority to someone else. It cannot recommend prices, which is the function of the corporation, but it can attach any recommendation it wishes to any item it refers to the minister. Ordinarily the minister will pass on that recommendation to the corporation. It might come as an instruction from the minister, passing on the recommendation to the board.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: But this committee is the really important body?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, no; the functions are different. Each has its own function, and I could not say which is the more important. Certainly the corporation has a tremendously important task in determining the methods of sale, in pricing the products and in setting up an organization for distribution across Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Does the minister anticipate that holding some of this material will be a very considerable operation?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The storage?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Does the committee decide that?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: No; the board will decide that. The committee may recommend that a certain item be held off the market. For example, the wartime prices and trade board has a representative on the committee. The committee may take the view on the recommendation of the wartime prices and trade board that it would not be beneficial to the Canadian economy to place a certain article on the market at this time. That recommendation would be passed on to the board, but ordinarily the board would be responsible for deciding when the material should be sold and at what price.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is provision made in this bill for the control and disposal of crown assets in Europe or anywhere else?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: In what way?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The board has jurisdiction over Canadian surplus materials wherever they may be. It has power to open bank accounts abroad, to appoint representatives or committees abroad, and to open offices abroad. As a matter of fact the board is represented in London; one of our munitions and supply officers in London is the representative of the board for any disposal in the United Kingdom.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: How about Italy and France and North Africa?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: That will come later.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is not the government of the United States setting up separate boards in those countries-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I dare say they are.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
-to dispose of their surplus stocks after the war, particularly to rush the disposal? And should we not be doing that also?

Surplus Crown Assets

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: We have no problems in those countries at the moment. Any supplies we have in Italy are in the custody of the Canadian army in that country, and they are not surplus. If they should become surplus I daresay the army will find some way of disposing of them for value.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: At page 3646 of Hansard the minister said this crown assets allocation committee would review the statements of the various government departments in regard to surplus assets, as to whether or not they were really surplus to the requirements of the particular department.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Not of the particular department; of the government as a whole.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Very well. I should think there would be just as much need for a corresponding provision for review as to whether or not certain departments were holding back in reserve assets which were not needed. It might be that certain departments of national defence would find themselves with a great deal of material which in the eyes of some of their officers would be useful as a reserve, but if they were reviewed by a proper authority-perhaps this board or perhaps some other committee of the cabinet-they would be found to be surplus. I am wondering whether it would not be well to insert in this bill some provision whereby not only the assets reported would be reviewed but it could be found out exactly what assets which might be surplus were still in the hands of various departments.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The minister of each department must be the judge of whether or not he has surplus material in his department. The officer representing the department on the committee is impressed with the desirability of not carrying surplus material, and I have no doubt he will exercise any influence he may have in the department in the direction of having surplus material reported to the board. But a committee of this type, or any outside authority, can hardly go inside any particular department of government and instruct the minister or the department as to what should be disposed of and what should be kept.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Where will policy be made in regard to the operation of the Crown Assets Corporation? We have the minister, and it would appear from a reading of the bill that he has great power in a large number of cases. In fact, much of the decision seems to rest with him personally. Then we have the crown assets allocation committee, and then the officers of the War Assets Corporation.
Reverting to the question I asked this afternoon in regard to government policy with respect to the three billion dollars worth of surplus war assets which we may have after the war is over, will that amount or parts of it be withheld from the market so that ordinary business ma3' go ahead? That is a question of policy. That amount of three billions of dollars works out to about $300 for each man, woman and child. Many of those assets will, of course, be of a military nature, and of no possible civilian use. At the same time there will be a great deal of clothing and other items which could be converted to civilian use, and it will be a question of great concern to business men in this country to learn what is going to happen to those supplies, because on what is to happen to them will depend much of their planning for postwar employment. The minister gave me his answer, one which was not satisfactory to me. However I cannot force him to give a different one, if he does not care to do so.
Nevertheless I should like to learn from him this: With whom will that policy in connection with the disposal of surplus assets rest? Who will decide whether or not they will be thrown on the market, with the resulting dislocation of ordinary industry and ordinary workmen, or whether those surplus assets will be withheld from the market? Where would one expect to find that policy declared, as it must be declared, it seems to me, if business is to go ahead in the post-war period?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The Minister of Munitions and Supply has absolute authority over every purchase that is made, or has been made since the war began. But the Minister of Munitions and Supply has not made every purchase-has not made any purchase. He must see that he has an organization which functions reasonably, and along reasonable lines.
The Minister of Munitions and Supply bears the same relationship to the Crown Assets Corporation. He is responsible for the work of the corporation, and he exercises that responsibility through a board of directors of his own choosing, which he supposes to be competent to advise him in that relation. The board represents a cross-section of industry and consumers. I should think, if he were a wise minister, he would accept the judgment of that board on the larger questions of policy as well as on details. I think that should satisfy my hon. friend, if he will reflect on the whole situation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Which board will be advising? Is it to emanate from the minister,

Surplus Crown Assets

backed by the decision of those whom he considers worthy of advising him, or is it to come from the crown assets allocation committee? Or is it to come from the officers of the War Assets Corporation? I want to know where business men will find out the policy of this government at some time in the future, in regard to the disposal of surplus war assets.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: It is contained in section 9 of the bill.

Section agreed to.
On section 6-Term of office.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Section 6 states that the term of office of the crown assets allocation committee members shall be one year. Then the directors of the War Assets Corporation shall hold office for three years. In the United States their whole programme is based upon as short a term as possible. Is it expected that these gentlemen are to be in office for three years? It states that they are to be reappointed. Surely to goodness there will not be a long time intervening between the end of the war and the final disposition or final control of assets left over from the war. If it is to take a long time, then there will be a terrific cost by way of salaries of one kind and another.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The committee is appointed for one year. The reason is that it is an advisory committee, composed largely of government officers. The corporation is appointed for three years, with terms of two years and one year for certain directors. The purpose of that is to obtain continuity.
I feel certain that the work of the corporation will last for at least ten years. The last war ended in 1918, and we are still disposing of surplus material from it. Only the other day we sold some harness left from that war.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: But we did not keep a committee in office for ten years after the war.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I point out to the minister that there seems to be strange incongruity between sections 6 and 7. Although we have not yet reached section 7,
I refer to it for purposes of comparison. It states that "the committee shall advise the minister". In other words, this is an advisory committee. I suggest that subsection 2 of section 6 destroys the position of the advisory committee, because it says:
(2) The committee shall be responsible to, and subject to the direction and control of the minister.
I do not know whether the minister sees the humorous aspect, but it does seem to me 
that if ever there was a committee which was thoroughly under the control, guidance and direction of the minister, this is certainly the one. It ceases to have that independence which an advisory committee should have.
I point this out to the minister in the thought that he might wish to have subsection 2 deleted. I should think that would be done, if the committee is to serve any useful purpose in an advisory capacity. How can a committee advise the minister when the minister himself, according to the bill as it now stands, exercises over that committee complete direction and control? It seems to me that is not the relationship which should exist between an advisory committee and the minister in charge. So as to relieve himself of any charge of having taken a dictatorial attitude, I suggest that the minister might well reconsider subsection 2, if, indeed, he has not already done so.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I take it that the committee must be responsible to someone.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I have no objection to its being responsible.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I point out that the minister takes advice from a great many officers, for whom he is responsible. My hon. friend always likes to suggest some independent body that is responsible to no one. I could mention one or two organizations of that type, but 1 do not think they would be very helpful. The minister must take the responsibility. The government must take it ultimately, and the minister is responsible for advising the government.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is all right,

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The minister must get his
advice where he can get sound advice. He forms this committee, which he believes is capable of advising him as to whether material is really surplus to government requirements. It may be surplus to the requirements of one department, or it may be material that another department can use. However, it is the duty of the committee to make sure that no department of government requires that material. That is their first duty. Then the committee looks into certain aspects which are purely governmental. Is it required for relief purposes? Is it required for Mutual Aid? Is it required for any purpose allied with government? Then it has regard to other governments. Is it material of a class that the provinces should have first option on, and the municipalities second option? It calls all these matters of general policy to the attention of the minister. The committee makes a recommendation to the minister on each item. The

Surplus Crown Assets
duty of the committee ends there. I might point out that there is no relationship between the committee and the corporation. My hon. friend asks to whom business would go to deal with. It would go to the corporation; it would have nothing to do with the committee. The committee looks at things from the government viewpoint and the policy viewpoint. The actual selling is done by the corporation, and the corporation will be the only agency that will have any relationship with the public, or with business, or with anything else. The duty of the committee is to advise the minister.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think the minister
missed my point with respect to the question of responsibility. I did not intend to convey that criticism to the minister. If I did not succeed in making myself clear, perhaps I may do so now. I think it goes without saying that the committee would be responsible to the minister and I should think no one would raise an objection about that. My objection was that under subsection 2 the committee would be subject to the direction and control of the minister. That was the part of the section to which I objected. I can rightly understand that there must be responsibility, but when you give direction and control it seems to me that that takes away the real effect of an advisory committee.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I would point out to the leader of the opposition that there might be objection if it were the other way around. The minister could come into the house some day and say, "I am sorry; I have no control of the committee." If he said that, we in the opposition would state pretty clearly that we considered he was responsible.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I think the wording is correct. The minister may ask the committee to investigate any aspect of a transaction and the committee is bound to do so. The minister is responsible for the salaries paid the chairman, and to those members outside the government service.

Section agreed to.
Section 7 agreed to.
On section 8-Secretary and officers.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Will the secretary and other officials be taken out of the present civil service, or will this mean the establishment of a new staff?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The section states that the staff shall be appointed or employed in the manner authorized by law; that means through the civil service commission. In
100-237i
addition, the minister may temporarily employ such persons of technical or professional attainments as he may deem necessary, as well as other temporary employees.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The words "authorized by law" would bring these employees within the scope of the civil service?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.
