On section 9-Ministerial powers.
Mr, GRAYDON: I want to raise objection to the wording and the language of this section. I wish to know what was in the minister's mind, because I am quite sure that this bill bears the mark of the minister's handiwork. I should like to know his motive in phrasing this particular section which states that he may do certain things with specific or general authority from the governor in council. I am afraid the governor in council may be tempted or invited by this section to give a blanket cheque or blanket authority to the minister. If I may say so, I think the minister has already clothed himself with wider powers under this bill than are normally given to a minister of the crown. I should like to have the minister's answer on that point.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
There is certain general
authority given to the minister. For example, he can exercise his own authority in transactions amounting to not more than $15,000. He has general authority to turn over to the War Assets Corporation material which is classified as scrap. But if he wishes to dispose of a building costing more than $15,000 or any item costing more than $15,000, he must have specific authority from council. That is why specific and general authorities are both mentioned.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Where is the reference in the bill to the $15,000 limitation?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: That authority is given by order in council.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The minister receives tremendous powers under section 9, and I notice that, later on, powers similar in nature although not quite as extensive or numerous are given to the board. Would it not be possible under this section for the minister to set aside the board if he chose to do so?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
He could then proceed to exercise these powers.
Surplus Croim Assets

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes. Strangely enough, the authority is with the government. If the board makes a bad decision, the minister could certainly overrule it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: This section certainly embraces a lot of territory, as anyone who is acquainted with the complexities of industry will realize. I have heard an hon. member- not a member of the government-advocate that his town should be permitted to buy road machinery cheaply. That particular town happens to be a coal producing town which ships coal to Ontario. If such a policy were pursued I wonder how the employees here *would be able to buy the coal which would be shipped from that town. I hope that in the disposition of all this material the question of jobs which may be affected thereby will be considered. Those who are familiar with production know that since the war broke out the iron industry has increased 100 per cent, which means that there will be tremendous stocks of iron goods for sale. It will take almost dictatorial powers to control the sale of those surplus iron goods so as not to interfere with reemployment which will be very important after the war. The total capacity of electric power plants has increased very largely. The capacity is twenty-five per cent greater now, and before the war is over, production will be still higher. It is greater to-day than ever before. If machines are thrown on the market in a disorderly way- that is a very good expression-it would, of course, affect employment in the electric production business. The same applies to the aluminum business, which has gone up 500 per cent since the war broke out.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: By 1,100 per cent.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The official United States report which I have here says 500 per cent, but the minister may have later information. The figure I gave is for 1942. The magnesium business, new in this country, has grown by 100 times greater in the United States, and perhaps it is more than that now. I am not greatly opposed to dictatorial powers if they are required to prevent the flooding of the market with cheap material.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: It does appear that there is great power being placed in the hands of the minister by this section. I do not know whether all that is necessary or not. I am not a business man, and I do not understand very much about crown corporations. But when you read of all the power that is being given to the minister, and give him power "to do any *other thing", that means he is all-powerful.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Omnipotent.
tMr. Stirling.]

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
However, I will content myself with going on record with that observation. May I ask this question? By paragraph (a) the minister may:
.	.	. sell, exchange, lease, lend or otherwise
dispose of or deal with surplus crown assets either gratuitously or for a consideration.
Apparently something is to be given away, so that once again the government believes in something for nothing. Could the minister give us a case where that might be done? I can understand that obsolete machinery might be given to provincial governments or something like that. But it does seem to me that this section may lay the minister or the government open to a good deal of criticism. That seems to me quite a loophole in this bill. I do not suppose that the government would do anything that they should not do, but this does leave it open to somebody to carry on quite a racket. I do not think the minister would. I think the government is sincere in this legislation, but it does seem to me that there are quite a few loopholes in the bill. Certainly it does not seem to be water-tight. I do not want to get out of bed on the wrong side in the morning, but equally I do not like to get into bed on the wrong side at night. Would the minister throw some light on paragraph (a) ? What example can he give of where it might be advisable to give any assets away? I might like to get in on that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The army in Italy might very well have surplus foodstuffs or surplus equipment that might be very badly needed by the starving people of Greece just across the Adriatic, and under this paragraph the minister would have authority, if he received that advice, to instruct that the material be transferred to Greece as a gift to the Greek people. That is one application. It would be a matter of charity on a national scale.

Section agreed to.
On section 10-War Assets Corporation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I want to ask a question, and if I may refer to a subsection of another bill I can put my question more quickly. Section 7 of the bill to amend the Aeronautics Act provides:
No member of the board shall either directly or indirectly engage in manufacturing or selling aircraft or in the transport of goods or passengers by aircraft for hire or reward.
And so on. I am wondering if there should not be a parallel clause in this bill. My hon. friends . to the right, particularly the hon. member for Rosedale, are quite concerned lest business has not proper connections with this War Assets Corporation. My fear is

Invasion oj Western Europe
that the connections of business with it will be too good for the welfare of the country as a whole. I should like to see some independence on the part of the members of this very important board comparable with the independence which the' minister prescribes in the act for the aeronautics board to which I have just referred. Would the minister make a statement on that?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The two are quite different. The aeronautics board is a judicial board as well as an advisory board. It has certain judicial functions to perform which would be prejudiced if any member of the board were interested in the operation or manufacture of aircraft. In the case of this corporation the minister is responsible, and the board is responsible to the minister for exercising its best judgment. It is a type of judgment that can best be exercised if a man has practical experience in that line. For instance a mining man would be the best adviser on the disposal of mining machinery and a merchant would be the best adviser on the best method of merchandising. It is just as in the operation of war plants we obtain the services of a man familiar with the type of operation required. He may also be operating a plant of his own in a small way.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: But it; does seem to me that the powers of this corporation are greater than the functions of the committee. I felt, as the minister was speaking, that he was referring more to the work of the advisory committee than to the work of the corporation. Wider powers are set out in section 12.
